Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 먹다 also becomes 먹고 싶어요 (want), 먹을 수 있어요 (can), and 못 먹어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then bend it.

conjugationTips.title: Describing a noun: ㄴ/은 vs ㄹ/을
conjugationTips.body: To put 좋다 in front of a noun, use the ㄴ/은 form for how something is right now: 좋은 것 ("a good / to like thing"). The ㄹ/을 form points to something that will or might become that way later. So 뜨거운 물 is water that is hot now, but 뜨거울 물 is water that will be hot — same adjective, different time feeling. For everyday description, reach for the ㄴ/은 form.

entries.shortExplanation: 당황하다 means "to be flustered" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 당황하다 (danghwanghada) means "to be flustered". Start from the polite form 당황해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 당황하다. A strong first sentence is 당황하지 마 ("Don't panic / Keep your cool"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 당황하다 also becomes 당황하고 싶어 (want), 당황할 수 있어 (can), and 당황 못 해 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 당황해요. Then practice 당황 안 해 vs 당황 못 해, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.
survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.note: Said when someone freezes up or gets caught off guard.

examples.en: They suddenly asked me in English so I totally froze.
examples.note: Very relatable for a foreigner-in-Korea scenario, reversed — being put on the spot.

examples.en: My card got declined and I panicked at the checkout.
examples.note: 계산대 = the cashier/checkout counter; everyday convenience-store/cafe vocab.

examples.en: When I get flustered, no Korean comes out at all.
examples.note: 안 나오다 here = 'doesn't come out (of my mouth)', natural for forgetting words.

entries.nuance: 당황하다 = to be momentarily flustered, thrown off, caught off guard (not long-term panic). It's the perfect word for those 'my brain went blank' moments. 당황스럽다 (adjective) describes a situation as 'awkward/bewildering'. The passive-ish 당황하다 already covers the felt experience, so 당황돼 is non-standard — use 당황했어.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 당황하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 당황해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 당황돼 — unlike 걱정/긴장, 당황하다 is not commonly used with 되다; stick to 당황해 / 당황했어.

lesson.canDo: Use 당황해요 in a real beginner sentence, then change it into want, can, cannot, and have-to forms without losing the basic meaning.
studyFlow: Say 당황해요 first. This is the safest spoken form for most beginner situations.
Add one useful frame: 당황하지 마. Read the Hangul first, then check the romanization.
Practice the contrast between 당황 안 해 and 당황 못 해.
Open one linked pattern and come back to this card to see the same grammar in a verb form.
lesson.teacherNote: Do not ask a beginner to memorize all 15 forms at once. Teach 당황해요 first, then add one communicative need: desire (당황하고 싶어), possibility (당황할 수 있어), or limitation (당황 못 해).
lesson.pronunciationTip: 당황하다 is written danghwanghada. In real sentences, compare the audio with the romanization because Korean sound changes can cross syllable blocks.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 당황해요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 당황하다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place

examples.note: Relatable dating wisdom; 관계 = relationship, ~만 ...면 안 돼 = 'it won't do if only...'.

entries.shortExplanation: 버티다 means "to hold out" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.en: Just hold on a little longer
usagePhrases.note: Gritty encouragement — survive the hard part.

examples.en: I got through exam season running on coffee.
examples.note: ~(으)로 버티다 = 'get by on'; 시험 기간 = exam period. Universal student life.

examples.en: My boss was awful so I held out a year and then quit.
examples.note: 진상 = a nasty/awful person (slang); 퇴사하다 = 'to quit one's job'.

examples.ko: 여기서 포기하지 말고 끝까지 버텨 보자.
examples.romanization: yeogiseo pogihaji malgo kkeutkkaji beotyeo boja.
examples.en: Don't give up here — let's tough it out to the end.
examples.note: 끝까지 = 'to the very end'; pairs naturally with 포기하지 말다.

entries.nuance: 버티다 = to hold out, hang on, endure/survive a hard stretch — often financially or against pressure (a tough job, no money, exam season). entries.shortExplanation: 위로하다 means "to comfort" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 위로하다 (wirohada) means "to comfort". Start from the polite form 위로해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 위로하다. A strong first sentence is 위로해 줘서 고마워 ("Thanks for comforting me"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 위로하다 also becomes 위로하고 싶어 (want), 위로할 수 있어 (can), and 위로 못 해 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

examples.romanization: chinguga himdeul ttae yeopeseo wirohae jwosseo.
examples.en: My friend comforted me when I was going through a hard time.
examples.note: 옆에서 ('by my side') + 위로해 주다 ('comfort me') — the giving form 주다 is almost always attached.

examples.ko: 말없이 안아주는 게 제일 큰 위로였어.
examples.romanization: mareopsi anajuneun ge jeil keun wiroyeosseo.
examples.en: Just being hugged without words was the biggest comfort.
examples.note: 위로 as a noun ('comfort'); 말없이 = 'without words', 안아주다 = 'to hug (someone)'.

examples.ko: 오늘 같은 날엔 치맥이 최고의 위로지.
examples.romanization: oneul gateun naren chimaegi choegoui wiroji.
examples.en: On a day like today, chicken and beer is the best comfort.
examples.note: 치맥 = 치킨+맥주 (fried chicken + beer), the iconic Korean comfort combo; ~지 = knowing agreement.

entries.nuance: 위로하다 = to comfort/console someone going through pain or loss. In practice it almost always appears as 위로해 주다 (comfort someone — with the benefactive 주다) or as the noun 위로 (위로가 되다 'to be a comfort', 위로를 받다 'to be comforted'). It's warm and a bit emotionally weighty — for everyday cheering-up you might lean on 응원하다 instead. 치맥 as 위로 is peak Korean culture.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 위로하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 위로해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Dropping the benefactive 주다 — 'I comforted my friend' is 친구를 위로해 줬어, not just 친구를 위로했어 (which sounds clinical/detached).

entries.shortExplanation: 응원하다 means "to cheer on" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to cheer on" in Korean is 응원하다 (eungwonhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 응원해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 응원하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 항상 응원할게 ("I'll always be rooting for you") — then reshape the same stem into 응원하고 싶어 (desire), 응원할 수 있어 (ability), and 응원 못 해 (a real limit) as the moment needs. usagePhrases.en: I'll always be rooting for you
usagePhrases.note: Warm, supportive send-off; common in messages and goodbyes.

examples.en: I'm rooting for your new job to go well!
examples.note: 잘되길 (= 잘되기를) 응원하다 = 'cheer for it to go well'; sweet, everyday support.

examples.en: I'm always on your side and rooting for you.
examples.note: 네 편이다 = 'to be on your side'; pairs naturally with 응원하다.

examples.ko: 손흥민 경기 있어서 친구들이랑 모여서 응원했어.
examples.romanization: sonheungmin gyeonggi isseoseo chingudeurirang moyeoseo eungwonhaesseo.
examples.en: There was a Son Heung-min match so we gathered to cheer.
examples.note: 응원하다 also = cheering for a sports team; 모이다 = 'to gather'. Football-watch culture.

entries.nuance: 응원하다 = to cheer on / root for / support — both literally (a sports team) and emotionally (a friend's goals). For everyday encouragement, 응원해 / 응원할게 is lighter and more upbeat than 위로하다 (which is for someone in pain). Telling someone 응원할게 is one of the warmest, most natural things to say. Often takes the benefactive 응원해 줘 when asking for support.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 응원하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 응원해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

usagePhrases.note: Caring phrase to a loved one

examples.en: Even when busy, I always make sure to eat breakfast.

examples.ko: 혼자 살면 끼니 챙겨 먹기 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: honja salmyeon kkini chaenggyeo meokgi himdeureoyo.

examples.ko: 요즘 일이 많아서 밥을 잘 못 챙겨 먹어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum iri manaseo babeul jal mot chaenggyeo meogeoyo.
examples.en: I've been so busy lately I can't eat properly.

entries.nuance: 챙겨 먹다 means to deliberately take care to eat (not skip meals), built from 챙기다 ('to look after') plus 먹다. 밥 잘 챙겨 먹어 is one of the warmest, most common things Koreans say to show they care, like a parent texting a kid. You'll also see it written without the space (챙겨먹다), but the standard spelling separates the two words.

entries.explanation: 다치다 (dachida) means "to get hurt". Start from the polite form 다쳐요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 다치다. A strong first sentence is 어디 다쳤어요? usagePhrases.note: First thing people ask if you limp in or hold an injured spot.

examples.en: I hurt my knee while playing soccer.
examples.note: V-다가 = 'while doing X, (something happened)'; super common with injuries.

examples.en: I fell and hurt my wrist a little.
examples.note: 손목 = wrist; useful to name the exact body part at a clinic (정형외과).

examples.en: It's not a serious injury.
examples.note: 크게 다치다 = 'to be badly hurt'; reassuring a worried friend or doctor.

entries.nuance: 다치다 covers any physical injury to yourself — bumps, cuts, sprains, breaks — and the body part takes 을/를 (무릎을 다쳤어요). It's intransitive in feel ('I got hurt'), not 'I hurt someone', so don't use it to describe injuring another person. At a hospital, pairing 다치다 with the exact body part (발목, 허리, 손목) gets you to the right department fast.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 다치다 as a complete polite sentence.

entries.nuance: 낫다 ('heal') is a ㅅ-irregular verb: the ㅅ disappears before a vowel (나아요, 나았어요, 나을), but stays before a consonant (낫습니다, 낫고). examples.note: 삐다 almost always takes 발목 (ankle) or 손목 (wrist) as the object with 을/를.

examples.en: I sprained my ankle so I put on a pain patch.
examples.note: 파스 = medicated pain patch, sold at every 약국 (pharmacy); 붙이다 = to stick on.

examples.en: When you sprain it, ice it.
examples.note: 찜질하다 = to apply a hot/cold compress; standard first-aid advice.

entries.nuance: 삐다 is the everyday verb for spraining a joint, overwhelmingly used with 발목 (ankle) and 손목 (wrist). For a clinic visit, 발목을 삐었어요 plus '부었어요' (it's swollen) communicates the whole problem clearly.

entries.nuance: 긁다 is the physical act of scratching with nails or an object, and it pairs naturally with the adjective 가렵다 ('to be itchy'): 가려워서 긁어요 ('it itches so I scratch'). usagePhrases.note: Crucial phrase for food poisoning, a hangover, or motion sickness.

examples.note: 상하다 = to go bad/spoil; -았는지 = 'whether (I)... '. Key for a clinic visit.

entries.nuance: 토하다 is the direct verb for vomiting and is fine to use at a clinic or pharmacy. The hedged 토할 것 같아요 ('I feel like I might throw up') is what you say while it's still coming on. A softer, very common alternative is 게우다, and Koreans also describe nausea with 속이 안 좋다 ('my stomach is off') or 메스껍다 ('to feel queasy'). entries.shortExplanation: 앓다 means "to be sick with / to suffer from" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

examples.note: -(으)시- honorific for elders: 앓다 → 앓으셨어요. 병을 앓다 = to suffer from a disease.

examples.en: I'm suffering from a mental/emotional struggle because of stress.
examples.note: 마음의 병 = 'illness of the heart'; 앓다 extends to emotional suffering.

entries.nuance: 앓다 means to be down with or suffer through an illness over a period, and it takes the sickness as a direct object (감기를 앓다, 독감을 앓다) — unlike 아프다, which just describes that something hurts. It carries a heavier, more drawn-out feeling, so it fits flu, chronic disease, or even emotional pain (마음의 병을 앓다). The reduplicated 끙끙 앓다 paints someone groaning or quietly agonizing. In casual daily talk people still say 아팠어요 more often; 앓다 sounds a notch more serious or literary.

examples.ko: 푹 쉬어야 빨리 회복할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: puk swieoya ppalli hoebokal su isseoyo.
examples.en: You can only recover fast if you rest well.
examples.note: A-/V-아야 = 'only if'; the must-rest message Koreans repeat constantly.

examples.note: 체력 = stamina/physical strength; 영양제 = supplements; 챙겨 먹다 = to be sure to eat.

entries.nuance: 회복하다 is the slightly formal verb for recovering — from illness, surgery, fatigue, or even a bad mood (기분을 회복하다 is rarer; 컨디션을 회복하다 is common). It takes what you regain as an object: 건강을/체력을/컨디션을 회복하다. For everyday 'I got better', Koreans more often say 나았어요 (from 낫다); 회복하다 sounds more clinical and fits doctors, recovery periods, and written notes. The noun 회복 ('recovery') shows up on hospital discharge papers and sick-leave messages.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 회복하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 회복해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Treating it as intransitive — you recover something: 건강을 회복하다 (object). Saying just 회복했어요 is fine in context, but '몸이 회복했어요' is better as '몸이 회복됐어요' (passive) or '컨디션을 회복했어요'.

entries.explanation: 삼키다 (samkida) means "to swallow". Start from the polite form 삼켜요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 삼키다. entries.nuance: 삼키다 is the verb for swallowing food, drink, pills, or saliva, and what you swallow takes 을/를. It's genuinely useful at a pharmacy or clinic — '약을 삼키기 힘들어요' (hard to swallow pills) or '침 삼킬 때 아파요' (hurts when I swallow) precisely describe throat problems. Figuratively it also means holding something back (눈물을 삼키다 = to swallow one's tears, 화를 삼키다 = to swallow one's anger), which you'll hear in dramas.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 삼키다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 삼켜요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

usagePhrases.note: 튀기다 = cook submerged in hot oil. The noun 튀김 names dishes like 새우튀김, 야채튀김.

examples.en: I deep-fried the shrimp until crispy.
examples.note: 바삭하게 (until crispy) is the classic result phrase for 튀기다; past is 튀겼어요.

examples.en: I deep-fry french fries myself.
examples.note: 튀겨 먹다 = fry (something) and eat it; common 'cook-it-yourself' pattern.

examples.en: The oil is hot, so be careful when deep-frying.
examples.note: 튀길 때 = when deep-frying; a natural safety reminder.

entries.nuance: 튀기다 is a regular verb (튀겨요, 튀겼어요) for cooking food submerged in plenty of hot oil. Keep it separate from 볶다 (stir-fry, little oil, constant tossing) and 부치다 (shallow pan-fry flat foods). The 튀김 noun form is everywhere in markets and 분식 shops, so recognizing the verb helps you order. It's also used for 'to bounce' a ball, but the cooking meaning dominates in daily life.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 튀기다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 튀겨요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Mixing up 튀기다 (deep-fry, lots of oil) with 볶다 (stir-fry, little oil).
Spelling it 튀기다 but conjugating as 튀기어요 — the correct contracted form is 튀겨요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 튀기다 becomes 튀길 수 있어요 ("can") and 튀길 거예요 ("will"). entries.english: to boil (a liquid) / to make (soup, stew, ramyeon)
entries.shortExplanation: 끓이다 means "to boil (a liquid) / to make (soup, stew, ramyeon)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 끓이다 (kkeurida) means "to boil (a liquid) / to make (soup, stew, ramyeon)". Start from the polite form 끓여요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 끓이다. A strong first sentence is 라면을 끓이다 ("to make ramyeon"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 끓이다 also becomes 끓이고 싶어요 (want), 끓일 수 있어요 (can), and 끓일 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: The set phrase for cooking instant ramyeon. Koreans never say 라면을 만들다 for cooking it — it's always 끓이다.

examples.en: Shall I make you some ramyeon?
examples.note: 끓여 줄까요? — offering to cook ramyeon, an extremely common everyday line.

examples.en: I made soybean-paste stew.

examples.en: I'll boil the water first.
examples.note: 끓일게요 — announcing your next cooking step.

entries.nuance: 끓이다 is the causative pair of 끓다 ('to be boiling'): you 끓이다 a liquid to make it 끓다. Use it for boiling water and, crucially, for making soups, stews, and ramyeon — 라면을 끓이다 is fixed usage. The key contrast for learners is 삶다 (boil a solid food in water) vs 끓이다 (boil a liquid / make a brothy dish). Conjugates regularly: 끓여요, 끓였어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 끓이다 as a complete polite sentence.

Using 끓이다 to boil eggs or noodles — that solid-in-water sense is 삶다.

entries.explanation: "to blanch / to parboil (briefly)" in Korean is 데치다 (dechida). usagePhrases.note: Step one of most 나물 side dishes: quickly boil greens, then drain and season (무치다).

examples.en: I quickly blanched the bean sprouts.
examples.note: 데쳤어요 = past of 데치다 (ㅣ+어 → ㅕ); pairs with 살짝.

examples.en: Please blanch the broccoli in boiling water.
examples.note: 끓는 물에 데치다 = the standard blanching instruction.

examples.en: Shall I blanch the greens?
examples.note: 데칠까요? — offering to do the blanching step.

entries.nuance: 데치다 means a quick blanch — dropping vegetables (or sometimes squid) into boiling water for just seconds to soften them and lock in color, then draining. It's a prep step, not full cooking, and is the gateway to Korean 나물 banchan: 데치다 then 무치다 (season). Don't confuse it with 데우다 (to reheat already-cooked food), which sounds similar but is unrelated. Conjugates 데쳐요, 데쳤어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 데치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 데쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 데치다 (blanch in boiling water) with 데우다 (reheat food).
Treating 데치다 as full boiling — it's only a brief dunk; longer cooking is 삶다/끓이다.

entries.shortExplanation: 무치다 means "to season and toss (by hand) / to dress (a salad/namul)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 무치다 (muchida) = "to season and toss (by hand) / to dress (a salad/namul)". examples.note: 무쳤어요 = past; 참기름에 무치다 is the quintessential namul finish.

entries.nuance: 무치다 is the hands-on tossing that finishes most Korean banchan: you blanch (데치다) a vegetable, then 무치다 it with seasoning until evenly coated. Don't mix it up with 비비다 (to mix by stirring, like bibimbap) — 무치다 specifically means dressing/coating, often by hand.

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

entries.english: to slice / to cut (food, on a board)
entries.shortExplanation: 썰다 means "to slice / to cut (food, on a board)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 썰다 (sseolda) means "to slice / to cut (food, on a board)". Start from the polite form 썰어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 썰다. A strong first sentence is 야채를 썰다 ("to slice vegetables"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 썰다 also becomes 썰고 싶어요 (want), 썰 수 있어요 (can), and 썰 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 썰어요. Then practice 안 썰어요 vs 썰 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

usagePhrases.en: I slice / to cut (food, on a board).
I do not slice / to cut (food, on a board).
I want to slice / to cut (food, on a board).
I can slice / to cut (food, on a board).
I have to slice / to cut (food, on a board).

usagePhrases.note: 썰다 is the cooking-specific 'cut' — slicing food on a cutting board (도마). More natural than 자르다 in the kitchen.

examples.en: Please slice the green onion into thin rounds.
examples.note: 송송 썰다 = mince into little rounds, a set kitchen phrase; 썰어 주세요 to ask for it.

examples.en: I cut the meat into bite-sized pieces.
examples.note: 썰었어요 = past (ㄹ stem keeps ㄹ before 어); 한입 크기 = bite-size.

examples.en: Shall I slice the onions?
examples.note: 썰까요? — the ㄹ drops before ㄹ/ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ, hence 썰까 (not 썰을까).

entries.nuance: 썰다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the ㄹ disappears before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ endings (썹니다, 써세요) but stays before vowel endings (썰어요, 썰었어요). In the kitchen 썰다 is far more natural than the general 자르다 (already in your deck) for slicing food on a board. Learn it with the cutting adverbs — 얇게, 채 썰다 (julienne), 어슷, 송송 — which appear constantly in recipes.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 썰다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 썰어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Keeping the ㄹ in front of ㅂ/ㅅ — it's 썹니다 and 써세요, not 썰습니다/썰으세요.
Using 자르다 for everything; in cooking, slicing food is more naturally 썰다.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 썰어 and 썰어요 together.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 야채를 썰다. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 안 썰어요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 썰 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.body: Once 썰어요 feels easy, practice 썰고 싶어요, 썰 수 있어요, and 썰어야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

entries.shortExplanation: 다지다 means "to mince / to finely chop" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to mince / to finely chop" in Korean is 다지다 (dajida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 다져요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 다지다 for study notes. usagePhrases.note: 다진 마늘 (minced garlic) is in almost every Korean recipe; you can even buy it pre-minced at the mart.

examples.en: I finely minced the garlic and onion.
examples.note: 잘게 다지다 = mince finely; 다졌어요 is the past.

examples.en: Please mince some ginger too.
examples.note: 다져 주세요 — asking for an ingredient to be minced.

examples.en: Shall we make patties with the minced meat?
examples.note: 다진 고기 = ground meat; shows the attributive form in real use.

entries.nuance: 다지다 means chopping something into very fine pieces — finer than 썰다. It shows up constantly as the attributive 다진 (다진 마늘, 다진 고기) in recipes and on product labels, so it's worth recognizing even before you cook much. Conjugates regularly: 다져요, 다졌어요. The same verb metaphorically means 'to firm up / consolidate' (기초를 다지다), but the kitchen sense is what you'll use daily.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 다지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 다져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 다지다 (mince, very fine) with 썰다 (slice into pieces).
Forgetting the attributive 다진 — say 다진 마늘, not 다지는 마늘, for 'minced garlic'.

entries.english: to mix together (by stirring) / to rub
entries.shortExplanation: 비비다 means "to mix together (by stirring) / to rub" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 비비다 (bibida) = "to mix together (by stirring) / to rub". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 비벼요 plus one useful sentence like 밥을 비비다 ("to mix rice (into bibimbap)"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 비비고 싶어요 for what you want, 비빌 수 있어요 for what you can, 비빌 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together.

I do not mix together (by stirring) / to rub.
I want to mix together (by stirring) / to rub.
I can mix together (by stirring) / to rub.
I have to mix together (by stirring) / to rub.

usagePhrases.note: 비비다 is the verb hiding in 비빔밥 — you 밥을 비벼 먹어요, stirring rice with toppings and gochujang.

examples.en: Add gochujang and mix it well before eating.
examples.note: 비벼서 드세요 = mix it and then eat; the standard bibimbap instruction.

examples.en: I added sesame oil and mixed it.
Shall we mix the spicy noodles together?
examples.note: 비빌까요? — proposing to do the mixing; note the pun-like 비빔/비비다 pairing.

entries.nuance: 비비다 means mixing by stirring and tossing everything together — it's literally the root of 비빔밥 and 비빔국수. The key contrast for cooks is 비비다 (stir everything together evenly, like bibimbap) vs 무치다 (dress/coat an ingredient with seasoning, usually a side dish). It conjugates regularly (비벼요, 비볐어요) and also means 'to rub' (눈을 비비다) in non-food contexts. A super practical word at any Korean table.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 비비다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 비벼요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 비비다 (stir/mix together) with 무치다 (season/dress an ingredient).
Writing 비비어요 instead of the contracted 비벼요.

entries.english: to cool (something) down / to let cool
entries.shortExplanation: 식히다 means "to cool (something) down / to let cool" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 식히다 (sikhida) means "to cool (something) down / to let cool". Start from the polite form 식혀요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 식히다. A strong first sentence is 국을 식히다 ("to cool the soup down"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 식히다 also becomes 식히고 싶어요 (want), 식힐 수 있어요 (can), and 식힐 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I cool (something) down / to let cool.
I do not cool (something) down / to let cool.
I want to cool (something) down / to let cool.
I can cool (something) down / to let cool.
I have to cool (something) down / to let cool.

usagePhrases.note: 식히다 is the causative of 식다 ('to cool off'): you 식히다 hot food so it 식다. Useful before serving kids or eating.

examples.ko: 국이 너무 뜨거우니까 좀 식혀서 드세요.
examples.romanization: gugi neomu tteugeounikka jom sikyeoseo deuseyo.
examples.en: The soup is too hot, so let it cool a bit before eating.
examples.note: 식혀서 드세요 — telling someone to let it cool; pairs with 뜨겁다.

examples.en: I let the bread cool for a moment.
examples.note: 한 김 식히다 = let the steam/heat off briefly; 식혔어요 is the past.

examples.en: Shall I cool the coffee down a bit?
examples.note: 식힐까요? — offering to cool a hot drink before someone drinks it.

entries.nuance: 식히다 is the causative/transitive partner of 식다: 식다 means food cools by itself, while 식히다 means you actively cool it (blowing on it, leaving it out, fanning it). It conjugates regularly (식혀요, 식혔어요) and is genuinely useful at the table — telling someone 식혀서 드세요 ('let it cool before eating') is caring and natural. Don't mix it with 식다, which can't take an object.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 식히다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 식혀요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using intransitive 식다 with an object — say 국을 식히다, not 국을 식다.
Confusing 식히다 (cool down) with 시키다 (to order food / make someone do) — similar sound, totally different meaning.

entries.nuance: 옮기다 is the everyday transitive verb for relocating an object — you physically pick it up and set it down somewhere else. It's transitive, so you need an object: 짐을 옮겨요, not just 옮겨요 with no context.

entries.nuance: 끌다 covers dragging something along the ground (a suitcase, a chair) and, figuratively, drawing attention or dragging out time. entries.nuance: 던지다 is the standard verb for throwing or tossing something through the air. entries.nuance: 떨어뜨리다 is the causative/transitive form of 떨어지다 (to fall): you accidentally let something fall. entries.nuance: 피하다 means to avoid, dodge, or steer clear of something — a person, a situation, bad weather, or a time of day. It can be physical (dodging a car) or social (avoiding someone).

entries.nuance: 넘기다 is the transitive partner of 넘다 (to cross over): you make something go over or past. entries.nuance: 내려놓다 combines 내리다 (to bring down) + 놓다 (to place), meaning to lower something from your hands and set it down. It's the natural opposite of 들어올리다. entries.nuance: 뒤집다 means to flip something to its other side or turn it inside out — flipping grilling meat, turning clothes for the wash, or upending a situation. commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 뒤집다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 뒤집어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
This is NOT a ㅂ-irregular: it's 뒤집어요 / 뒤집습니다, never '뒤지워요'. The ㅂ stays put.
뒤집다 is transitive (you flip it); for something that flips/capsizes by itself, use the passive 뒤집히다.

entries.english: to lean on, to rely on
entries.shortExplanation: 기대다 means "to lean on, to rely on" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to lean on, to rely on" in Korean is 기대다 (gidaeda). examples.note: Very common on buses and subways in Korea.

entries.nuance: 기대다 means to lean your body against something for support, and by extension to rely on someone. The particle is 에 for objects (벽에 기대다) and 에게/한테 for people (친구한테 기대다). It carries a warm nuance when emotional — 기대도 돼 ('you can lean on me') is a comforting thing to say. Don't confuse it with the homophone-ish 기대하다 (to expect/look forward to).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 기대다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 기대요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse 기대다 (to lean/rely) with 기대하다 (to expect). 기대돼요 = I'm excited/expecting; 기대요 = I lean on.
Use the particle 에 for surfaces: 벽에 기대다, not '벽을 기대다'.

entries.nuance: 누르다 is the go-to verb for pressing or pushing buttons — elevators, doorbells, app icons, the 'like' button. It is a 르-irregular verb: before a vowel ending the stem becomes 눌ㄹ-, giving 눌러요 and 눌렀어요. Master this pattern because daily life in Korea is full of buttons to press, and getting 눌러요 right immediately sounds natural.

For pushing a door or object (not a button), use 밀다; 누르다 is specifically pressing down on something.

entries.shortExplanation: 비키다 means "to step aside, to get out of the way" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

A strong first sentence is 죄송한데 잠깐만 비켜 주시겠어요? ("Sorry, could you step aside for a moment?"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 비키다 also becomes 비키고 싶어요 (want), 비킬 수 있어요 (can), and 비킬 수 없어요 (cannot). I do not step aside, to get out of the way.

I can step aside, to get out of the way.

usagePhrases.note: 비켜 주시겠어요? is the polite way to ask someone to move out of the way.

examples.en: A bike came from behind so I stepped to the side.

examples.note: Polite nudge to move; softer with 조금만.

examples.en: People cleared the way for the ambulance.

entries.nuance: 비키다 means to step aside or move out of someone's way. The polite request 비켜 주세요 / 비켜 주시겠어요? is essential for crowded subways, sidewalks, and elevators. On its own, a curt 비켜! is rude (like 'move it!'), so always soften it with 주세요 or 주시겠어요 unless you intend to be sharp. It's intransitive — you move yourself, not an object.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 비키다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 비켜요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Bare 비켜! sounds aggressive — always add 주세요/주시겠어요 to be polite in public.
비키다 is intransitive (you move aside); to move an OBJECT out of the way, use 치우다 or 옮기다.

entries.nuance: 판단하다 means to assess a situation and form a conclusion or decision — it's more analytical than emotional. entries.nuance: 예상하다 is to anticipate or predict an outcome based on reasoning — what you think will happen. It's neutral and works for weather, traffic, exam results, or business forecasts. usagePhrases.en: I had it wrong / I was mistaken
usagePhrases.note: the polite, blame-free way to admit you misremembered or mixed something up

examples.en: I mistakenly thought today was Saturday.
examples.note: N인 줄 착각하다 = wrongly think that it's N; the key pattern for a mistaken belief

examples.en: Sorry, I mistook you for someone else.
examples.note: A를 B로 착각하다 = mistake A for B; 으로/로 marks who you confused them with

examples.en: I thought the appointment was tomorrow, but I was mistaken.
examples.note: 착각이었어요 = it was a mistake (noun form); a natural way to wrap up admitting an error

entries.nuance: 착각하다 is to hold a mistaken belief or impression — you were sure of something that turned out to be wrong (the date, a person's identity, what someone meant). usagePhrases.note: a direct way to ask if someone suspects you; the object takes 을/를

examples.en: I can guess what's going on just from your expression.

entries.nuance: 짐작하다 is to make an educated guess or surmise based on limited clues — you infer something rather than know it for sure. It's softer and more reasoned than a wild guess: you're reading the signs. commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 짐작하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 짐작해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 짐작하다 for a random guess on a quiz — for picking an answer with no basis use 찍다; 짐작하다 implies you're inferring from clues

entries.shortExplanation: 떠올리다 means "to recall" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

Grow outward from one concrete line — 천천히 떠올려 보세요 ("Try to recall it slowly") — then reshape the same stem into 떠올리고 싶어요 (desire), 떠올릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 떠올릴 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

examples.note: N을/를 떠올리다 = call N to mind on purpose; 기억을 떠올리다 = recall a memory

examples.ko: 이 사진을 보면 옛날 생각을 떠올리게 돼요.
examples.romanization: i sajineul bomyeon yennal saenggageul tteoollige dwaeyo.
examples.en: Looking at this photo makes me recall the old days.
examples.note: -게 되다 = end up doing; 생각을 떠올리다 = bring a thought to mind

examples.en: I struggled to recall that person's name.
examples.note: 떠올리려고 애쓰다 = strain to remember; 떠올리려고 = trying to bring up

entries.nuance: 떠올리다 is the transitive partner of 떠오르다: you deliberately call a memory, image, or idea to mind (기억을 떠올리다 = you do the recalling), whereas with 떠오르다 the thought surfaces on its own (기억이 떠올라요). Use 떠올리다 + 을/를 when you're the one making the effort to remember. It's warmer and more vivid than 기억하다, which is plain 'to remember/retain.'

Use 떠올려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

entries.shortExplanation: 알아차리다 means "to notice" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

examples.en: Nobody noticed that I'd made a mistake.

examples.en: Only then did I notice something had gone wrong.
examples.note: 그제야 알아차리다 = notice only at that point; -다는 걸 reports what you noticed

entries.nuance: 알아차리다 is to notice or catch on — to suddenly become aware of something through perception (a change in mood, a mistake, someone's true intention). It's about detection, not analysis: you sense it and it registers. Compare 깨닫다 (to realize a fact or truth, often deeper): 알아차리다 is the quicker 'oh, I noticed that,' while 깨닫다 is the heavier 'I came to understand.'

I want to look back on.
I have to look back on.
I looked back on the past year
usagePhrases.note: a natural year-end reflection phrase; 지난 한 해 = the past year

examples.ko: 한국에서 보낸 시간을 되돌아보면 정말 많이 변했어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeseo bonaen siganeul doedorabomyeon jeongmal mani byeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Looking back on my time in Korea, I've really changed a lot.
examples.note: N을/를 되돌아보면 = when you look back on N; -보면 sets up a reflective conclusion

examples.en: Whenever things get hard, I look back on how I felt at the start.
examples.note: 처음 마음을 되돌아보다 = revisit your original feelings/intentions; 마다 = every time

examples.ko: 실수를 되돌아보고 다음엔 더 잘하려고 해요.
examples.romanization: silsureul doedorabogo daeumen deo jalharyeogo haeyo.
examples.en: I reflect on my mistakes and try to do better next time.
examples.note: 되돌아보고 = reflect and then; pairs with -(으)려고 하다 (intend to)

entries.nuance: 되돌아보다 is to reflect on or look back over the past — your year, your choices, a relationship — usually to draw a lesson or feeling from it. The 되- prefix adds a 'back again' nuance, making it more reflective than plain 돌아보다 (to turn and look). It's an introspective, slightly thoughtful word, perfect for journaling, year-end musings, or talking about how you've grown.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 되돌아보다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 되돌아봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using it for physically turning your head to look behind — that's 돌아보다 or 뒤를 돌아보다; 되돌아보다 is overwhelmingly about reflecting on the past

entries.shortExplanation: 바뀌다 means "to change, to be switched" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to change, to be switched" in Korean is 바뀌다 (bakkwida). usagePhrases.en: I do not change, to be switched.
I want to change, to be switched.
I can change, to be switched.
I have to change, to be switched.

usagePhrases.note: 바뀌다 = something changes on its own / gets switched. The thing that changes takes 이/가, not 을/를.

examples.en: The meeting time got changed to 3 o'clock.
examples.note: Super common at work — schedules, plans, and times 'get changed' on you.

examples.en: Oh, the shop's name changed.
examples.note: ~네요 adds a 'huh, I just noticed' tone — natural when you spot a change.

examples.en: The plan might change again.
examples.note: 또 (again) + 바뀌다 is the everyday way to warn that things aren't fixed yet.

entries.nuance: 바뀌다 is the intransitive partner of 바꾸다 — the thing that changes is the subject (이/가), and no one is named as the one doing it. Use 바꾸다 when YOU actively swap something (번호를 바꿨어요), and 바뀌다 when it simply ends up different (번호가 바뀌었어요). Spelling matters: it's 바뀌- (with 위), and the polite form is 바뀌어요, not 바껴요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 바뀌다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 바뀌어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 바뀌다 transitively — you can't say '번호를 바뀌었어요'. If YOU did it, use 바꾸다: 번호를 바꿨어요.
Don't write the polite form as 바껴요; the standard form is 바뀌어요 (the 바뀌- stem doesn't contract to 바껴-).

examples.en: Living here, my way of thinking has changed a lot.

examples.en: The rules will be different starting next year.
examples.note: Common in notices about policies, fees, or schedules changing.

entries.nuance: 달라지다 emphasizes that the result is now different from how it was, so it's the go-to verb for noticing change in someone's looks, mood, or a situation. It's intransitive, so don't attach 을/를: say 생각이 달라졌어요, not 생각을 달라졌어요.

entries.english: to increase, to grow, to stretch out
entries.shortExplanation: 늘어나다 means "to increase, to grow, to stretch out" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 늘어나다 (neureonada) means "to increase, to grow, to stretch out". Start from the polite form 늘어나요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 늘어나다. Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 늘어나다 means a quantity, number, or length gets bigger, and it feels a touch more concrete and visual than 늘다 — picture something physically stretching or a count climbing. examples.en: I got another pimple.
examples.note: For skin issues, bruises, etc.: 여드름이/멍이 생기다 ('a pimple/bruise forms').

examples.note: Casual but super common — 애인이/여자친구가 생기다 = 'to get a partner'.

examples.en: If a problem comes up, contact me right away.
examples.note: 문제가 생기다 = a problem arises; the conditional 생기면 is everyday phrasing.

entries.nuance: 생기다 covers a wide range: something coming into existence (가게가 생기다), an event/issue arising (일이/문제가 생기다), or a person 'getting' something they didn't have before (돈이/시간이/애인이 생기다). When canceling plans, '일이 생겼어요' is the natural excuse; learners often over-explain instead of using this set phrase.

entries.shortExplanation: 망가지다 means "to break down, to get ruined" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

examples.note: ~ㄴ 채로 = 'in a (ruined) state'; useful for complaints to delivery/sellers.

examples.en: My shoes got ruined from the rain.

entries.nuance: 망가지다 means something is damaged to the point it no longer works or holds its shape — broader than 고장나다 (which is mainly about machines failing). For pure machine malfunction, 고장났어요 is often more natural; reserve 망가지다 when there's real physical damage or 'wreckage'.

usagePhrases.note: 무너지다 = a structure caves in / crumbles down. The thing that collapses takes 이/가.

examples.en: The bridge collapsed in the heavy rain.
My plans collapsed in an instant.
examples.note: Figurative — plans, dreams, or systems 'falling apart'.

examples.en: My heart sank at that news.

entries.nuance: 무너지다 literally means a structure crumbles or caves in (a wall, building, bridge), but it's used just as often figuratively for emotions, plans, or order collapsing. Don't confuse the emotional 마음이 무너지다 (heart breaks) with mild disappointment; it's strong, for genuinely crushing moments.

usagePhrases.note: 멎다 = a flowing/ongoing natural thing ceases on its own. The thing that stops takes 이/가.

examples.note: Conditional 멎으면 = 'once it stops' — natural for weather.

examples.en: I was so startled my heart felt like it stopped.
examples.note: 심장이 멎다 = heart stops; the set phrase 멎는 줄 알았어요 = 'I thought it would stop'.

examples.en: The sound of rain stopped only after a long while.
examples.note: Slightly literary; 멎다 has a quieter, more natural feel than 멈추다.

entries.nuance: 멎다 means something flowing or continuous comes to a halt by itself — rain, snow, bleeding, a heartbeat. It's intransitive and never takes an object; for stopping a car or a machine you'd use 멈추다 or 세우다.

It's intransitive, so don't add 을/를: 피가 멎었어요 (the bleeding stopped), not 피를 멎었어요.

examples.en: The heat will continue into next week.
examples.note: Weather forecasts love this — 폭염이/장마가 이어지다.

examples.en: The meeting dragged on until evening.

entries.nuance: 이어지다 means something continues without breaking, or one thing connects into another — a road leading somewhere, weather persisting, a conversation flowing on, or a cause leading to a result (X로 이어지다). examples.en: It's right before my presentation, so my heart is racing.
examples.note: 심장이 두근거리다 and 가슴이 두근거리다 are interchangeable; 가슴 sounds slightly softer.

examples.ko: 내일 그 사람 만난다고 생각하니까 벌써 두근거려.
examples.romanization: naeil geu saram mannandago saenggakanikka beolsseo dugeungeoryeo.
examples.en: Just thinking about meeting them tomorrow, my heart's already fluttering.
examples.note: Casual 두근거려 to a close friend. 두근두근 is the matching mimetic word you'll see in texts.

examples.ko: 커피를 너무 많이 마셔서 가슴이 두근거렸어요.
examples.romanization: keopireul neomu mani masyeoseo gaseumi dugeungeoryeosseoyo.
examples.en: I drank too much coffee, so my heart was pounding.
examples.note: Also used literally for a physical racing heart from caffeine or running, not just emotion.

entries.nuance: 두근거리다 describes the physical sensation of a pounding or fluttering heart, so the grammatical subject is 가슴/심장, while the person is marked with -은/는 or a cause phrase. It covers the full range from giddy anticipation to nervous dread, which is why Koreans pair it with 설레다 for good nerves or 긴장되다 for bad ones to disambiguate. The mimetic 두근두근 shows up constantly in casual writing and captions.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 두근거리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 두근거려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 저는 두근거려요 to mean 'I'm excited' — the heart is the subject, so use 가슴이 두근거려요 (or 저는 설레요 if you mean the feeling).
Imperative/propositive forms like 두근거리세요 are grammatically possible but sound odd in real life, since you can't really order someone's heart to pound.

I can miss / to long for (someone or something absent).

examples.ko: 한국에 산 지 일 년 됐는데 가끔 엄마 음식이 그리워요.
examples.romanization: hanguge san ji il nyeon dwaenneunde gakkeum eomma eumsigi geuriwoyo.
examples.en: It's been a year living in Korea, and sometimes I miss my mom's cooking.
examples.note: ㅂ-irregular: 그립- + -어요 → 그리워요. Very common for expats describing home food.

examples.en: I really missed those days.
examples.note: Past tense 그리웠어요 for looking back nostalgically on a period of life.

examples.en: I missed my friend so much that I made a video call.
examples.note: 그리워서 (because I missed) drives an action. To say someone actively misses, switch to the verb 그리워하다.

entries.nuance: 그립다 is an adjective expressing your own felt longing, so what you miss is the subject (-이/가) and you cannot attach a direct object. Using 그립다 to say someone else misses something; switch to 그리워하다 (동생이 고향을 그리워해요).
notes: ㅂ: memorize 그리워 and 그리워요 together.

I do not be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed.
I want to be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed.
I can be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed.
I have to be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed.

usagePhrases.note: Covers two senses: bashful shyness (meeting new people) and embarrassment over a mistake. Tone and context separate them.

examples.ko: 사람들 앞에서 한국어로 말하는 게 아직 부끄러워요.
examples.romanization: saramdeul apeseo hangugeoro malhaneun ge ajik bukkeureowoyo.
examples.en: I'm still shy about speaking Korean in front of people.
examples.note: ㅂ-irregular: 부끄럽- + -어요 → 부끄러워요. A very relatable expat sentence.

examples.en: I made a mistake and was so embarrassed.
examples.note: Past 부끄러웠어요 for embarrassment over something you did.

examples.en: My younger sibling is shy around strangers.
examples.note: For describing someone else's shyness, use the verb 부끄러워하다 + object.

entries.nuance: 부끄럽다 spans shy bashfulness and self-conscious embarrassment, but it leans gentler and more inward than 창피하다, which is sharper public mortification. Because it's an adjective, your own feeling takes -이/가 on the cause, and describing another person's shyness requires the verb 부끄러워하다. The noun 부끄러움 means 'shyness' or 'shame' and shows up in more formal or written contexts.

entries.nuance: 창피하다 is the stronger, more public sibling of 부끄럽다 — it's the 'I want the floor to swallow me' feeling after you trip in front of a crowd or get scolded openly. entries.shortExplanation: 황당하다 means "to be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

examples.en: They suddenly said my reservation was canceled, so I was dumbfounded.
examples.note: 하다-verb: 황당하- + -았어요 → 황당했어요. Common in customer-service mishaps.

examples.en: His excuse was so absurd that I burst out laughing.
examples.note: 황당해서 (because it was absurd) leading to a reaction. Casual with a friend.

examples.en: They looked at me with a dumbfounded expression.
examples.note: 황당한 표정 ('a stunned/what-the-heck face') is a set phrase you'll hear a lot.

entries.nuance: 황당하다 captures the 'wait, what?' feeling when something is so unexpected or illogical it leaves you stunned — a baffling excuse, an out-of-nowhere cancellation, an absurd demand. Use 황당해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Translating it as plain 'surprised' (놀라다) — 황당하다 specifically implies the thing was absurd or nonsensical, not just unexpected.
Overusing it for mild surprises; save it for genuinely ridiculous situations.

entries.shortExplanation: 어이없다 means "to be flabbergasted / to find something absurd and senseless" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 어이없다 (eoieopda) means "to be flabbergasted / to find something absurd and senseless". Start from the polite form 어이없어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 어이없다. A strong first sentence is 진짜 어이없어 ("This is unbelievable / I can't even"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: The everyday reaction when something is so dumb or unfair it leaves you speechless. Extremely common in casual speech.

examples.en: Someone cut in line, so I was totally flabbergasted.
examples.note: 없다-type adjective: 어이없- + -었어요 → 어이없었어요. Note 길래 = 'because (I saw/noticed).'

examples.ko: 그 말 듣고 너무 어이없어서 헛웃음이 나왔어.

examples.en: After hearing that, I was so dumbfounded I let out a dry laugh.
examples.note: Pairs naturally with 헛웃음 (a hollow/dry laugh). Casual register.

examples.en: Stop with the ridiculous excuses.
examples.note: 어이없는 + noun ('a ludicrous ~'). 어이없는 변명/상황 are common collocations.

entries.nuance: 어이없다 (also said as 어이가 없다) is the punchy, everyday way Koreans react to something so absurd, unfair, or stupid that it stuns them into a speechless half-laugh. Compared with 황당하다, it carries a touch more exasperation or contempt — it's what you mutter when someone cuts in line or gives a nonsense excuse. Because 없다 behaves like an adjective, the third-person verb form is 어이없어하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 어이없다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 어이없어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spelling or hearing it as 어의없다 — the word is 어이 (no ㄴ/ㅢ); standard spelling is 어이없다.
Using it for pleasant surprise; 어이없다 is always negative — bafflement mixed with annoyance.

usagePhrases.note: For exhilarating moments — a roller coaster, a buzzer-beater, a sudden win. Has a sense of electric, tingling excitement.

examples.romanization: saengirinde yeollakdo an haeseo jom seopseopaesseoyo.
examples.en: It was my birthday and you didn't even text, so I felt a bit hurt.
examples.note: 하다-verb: 섭섭하- + -았어요 → 섭섭했어요. Classic mild-grievance use.

examples.en: Hearing you're already leaving makes me feel sad to see you go.
examples.note: Also expresses the bittersweet sadness of a goodbye, not just grievance. -네요 adds soft emotion.

examples.en: When you talk like that, it really hurts my feelings.
examples.note: Plain 섭섭하다 ending to a close friend, voicing gentle hurt.

entries.nuance: 섭섭하다 is a uniquely Korean shade of feeling: a gentle, wistful hurt or letdown when someone close to you doesn't meet your emotional expectations, or the bittersweet pang of parting. It's softer than 서운하다 (its near-synonym) only by nuance — many use them interchangeably — and much milder than anger or 화나다. Telling someone 섭섭해 signals 'you let me down a little,' inviting reassurance rather than confrontation.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 섭섭하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 섭섭해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Treating it as anger; 섭섭하다 is tender disappointment, so 화나다/짜증나다 are wrong for this feeling.
Using it about strangers — it implies a relationship close enough to have expectations.

entries.shortExplanation: 질리다 means "to be sick of / to get fed up with something" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 질리다 (jillida) means "to be sick of / to get fed up with something". Start from the polite form 질려요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 질리다. A strong first sentence is 이제 질렸어요 ("I'm sick of it now"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 질리다 also becomes 질리고 싶어요 (want), 질릴 수 있어요 (can), and 질릴 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

examples.ko: 매일 라면만 먹으니까 이제 진짜 질렸어요.
examples.romanization: maeil lamyeonman meogeunikka ije jinjja jillyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Eating only ramen every day, I'm really sick of it now.
examples.note: 이-stem verb: 질리- + -었어요 → 질렸어요. Marker -에 (라면에) is the textbook choice.

examples.en: I got fed up with the same routine, so I took off on a trip.
examples.note: 질려서 (fed up, so) → action. -에 marks the thing you tired of.

examples.ko: 그 노래 너무 많이 들어서 질릴 정도예요.
examples.romanization: geu norae neomu mani deureoseo jillil jeongdoyeyo.
examples.en: I've heard that song so much it's at the point of being sick of it.
examples.note: 질릴 정도 ('to the point of being fed up') is a useful set phrase.

entries.nuance: 질리다 is the everyday verb for being so over-saturated with something — a food, a routine, a song — that you can't stand any more of it. It also has a second, scarier sense: 질리다 can mean to turn pale or be paralyzed with fear (겁에 질리다, 새파랗게 질리다), so context matters. For the 'fed up' meaning, mark the source with -에 (most standard) or -이/가; English-speakers often wrongly add -을/를.

Use 질려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the source with -을/를; use -에 (라면에 질렸어요) or -이/가.
Forgetting the second meaning — 겁에 질리다 / 얼굴이 질리다 means to go pale with fear, not 'be bored.'

examples.en: It was a first date, so my heart was really fluttering.

entries.nuance: 설레다 is the warm, fluttery thrill of looking forward to something good — the butterflies before a date, a trip, or a fresh start. The standard dictionary form is 설레다 (past 설렜어요); you'll hear and see 설레이다/설레인다 everywhere, but those are nonstandard, so write 설레요/설렜어요. The matching noun 설렘 ('the flutter of excitement') is hugely popular in captions and song lyrics.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 설레다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 설레요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 설레이다 / 설레여요 / 설레임 — these are nonstandard; the correct forms are 설레다 / 설레요 / 설렘.
Confusing the contraction: 설레 + 었어요 = 설렜어요, not 설레었어요 in natural speech.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 설레다 becomes 설렐 수 있어요 ("can") and 설렐 거예요 ("will"). entries.english: to be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement
entries.shortExplanation: 들뜨다 means "to be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 들뜨다 (deultteuda) = "to be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 들떠요 plus one useful sentence like 완전 들떴어요 ("I'm totally hyped up"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 들뜨고 싶어요 for what you want, 들뜰 수 있어요 for what you can, 들뜰 수 없어요 for what you can't. I want to be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement.

I have to be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement.

usagePhrases.note: A buzzy, can't-sit-still excitement before something fun — a holiday, a concert, a trip. Often a bit giddier and more restless than 설레다.

examples.en: With the vacation coming up, everyone's all keyed up.
examples.note: ㅡ-irregular: 들뜨- + -어요 → 들떠요. 들떠 있다 = 'be in a giddy state.'

examples.en: Maybe because it's a long weekend, I felt giddy and restless.
examples.note: Past 들떴어요 (들뜨 + 었 → 들떴). The cause is often a holiday or event.

examples.en: Don't get too carried away — let's pack first.
examples.note: 들뜨지 말다 ('don't get over-excited'), often a gentle reminder to stay grounded.

entries.nuance: 들뜨다 is the bubbly, restless excitement that lifts your mood before something fun, but it carries a faint undertone of being so giddy you're a little distracted or unsettled — which is why 너무 들뜨지 마 ('don't get carried away') is a common caution. Compared with 설레다 (sweet, heart-fluttering anticipation), 들뜨다 is more buzzy and outwardly hyped. It conjugates as a ㅡ-irregular: 들뜨- + -어 → 들떠.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 들뜨다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 들떠요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Botching the ㅡ-drop: 들뜨- + -어요 is 들떠요, not 들뜨어요.
Assuming it's purely positive — it can hint at being overexcited or not thinking clearly, hence the 'don't get carried away' nuance.
notes: ㅡ: memorize 들떠 and 들떠요 together.

entries.english: to be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back
entries.shortExplanation: 주눅들다 means "to be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 주눅들다 (junukdeulda) means "to be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back". Start from the polite form 주눅들어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 주눅들다. A strong first sentence is 주눅들지 마세요 ("Don't let it intimidate you / don't shrink back"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 주눅들다 also becomes 주눅들고 싶어요 (want), 주눅들 수 있어요 (can), and 주눅들 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 주눅들어요. Then practice 주눅들지 않아요 vs 주눅들 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

I want to be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back.
I can be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back.
I have to be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back.
Don't let it intimidate you / don't shrink back
usagePhrases.note: Often used as encouragement. The phrase is built from 주눅(이) 들다, so you'll also see 주눅이 들다.

examples.ko: 한국어 실력이 부족해서 회의 때 자꾸 주눅들어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeo sillyeogi bujokaeseo hoeui ttae jakku junukdeureoyo.
examples.en: My Korean isn't good enough, so I keep getting cowed in meetings.
examples.note: ㄹ-irregular: before -ㅂ니다 the ㄹ drops → 주눅듭니다. A very real expat workplace feeling.

examples.en: I felt completely intimidated in front of the interviewer.
examples.note: Past 주눅들었어요. 주눅(이) 들다 literally means your spirit shrinks.

examples.en: Don't shrink back — speak up confidently.
examples.note: 주눅들지 말다 paired with 당당하게 ('confidently'), the opposite attitude. Common pep-talk.

entries.nuance: 주눅들다 (from 주눅(이) 들다) means to feel so intimidated or self-conscious that you shrink back, lose confidence, and can't assert yourself — a very useful word for the expat experience of freezing up in Korean meetings or formal settings. It's a ㄹ-irregular built on 들다, so the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ endings (주눅듭니다). The natural cure-words to pair it with are 당당하다 (be self-assured) and the encouragement 주눅들지 마.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 주눅들다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 주눅들어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Keeping the ㄹ before -ㅂ니다 (saying 주눅들습니다) — the ㄹ drops: 주눅듭니다.
Marking the cause with -을/를; use -에 (분위기에 주눅들다).
notes: ㄹ: memorize 주눅들어 and 주눅들어요 together.

entries.explanation: "to take out" in Korean is 꺼내다 (kkeonaeda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 꺼내요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 꺼내다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 가방에서 지갑을 꺼냈어요. ("I took my wallet out of my bag.") — then reshape the same stem into 꺼내고 싶어요 (desire), 꺼낼 수 있어요 (ability), and 꺼낼 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

examples.ko: 택배 박스에서 물건만 꺼내고 박스는 접어서 버려요.

examples.en: I take only the items out of the delivery box and fold the box to throw away.

entries.nuance: 꺼내다 is the default verb for taking something out of an enclosed space like a bag, pocket, fridge, or drawer. It contrasts with 빼다 (to pull/remove a fitted thing) — you 꺼내 a wallet from a bag but 빼 a key from a lock. It also means 'to bring up' a topic: 그 얘기 왜 꺼냈어? (Why did you bring that up?).

Use 꺼내요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 빼다 instead of 꺼내다 for taking things out of a bag — 빼다 implies pulling out something stuck or fitted, not retrieving from open space.

entries.nuance: 집다 means to pick something up with your fingers, chopsticks, or tongs — a precise grasp of a small object. entries.nuance: 담다 specifically means to put or load contents into a container — a bag, bowl, box, or shopping cart. Online, 장바구니에 담다 is the standard phrase for 'add to cart.' entries.nuance: 펴다 is the all-purpose verb for unfolding, spreading out, or straightening — opening a book, laying out bedding, opening an umbrella, or straightening your back. I want to help out / to lend a hand.
I can help out / to lend a hand.

usagePhrases.note: Offering to pitch in on a hands-on task like carrying or cleaning up.

examples.en: I'll help out moving the boxes.
examples.note: 거들다 fits physical helping-out; very natural for moving day among friends.

examples.en: Help your mom with the dishes a bit.
examples.note: 거들다 = chip in on a task someone else is already doing, rather than doing it for them.

examples.romanization: yeopeseo malloman geodeulji malgo jikjeop jom hae.

examples.note: 거들다 can also mean to add words/back someone up — here 'chiming in' without acting.

entries.nuance: 거들다 means to assist with something already in progress — to pitch in or lend a hand, often on physical or household tasks. It's lighter than 돕다 (to help) and implies you're a secondary helper, not the main doer. Note the ㄹ-irregular: ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ (거듭니다), but stays elsewhere (거들어요, 거들 거예요).

Use 거들어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the formal form as 거들습니다 — the ㄹ drops, so it's 거듭니다.
Treating 거들다 as full help; for serious help or rescue use 돕다, not 거들다.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 거들어 and 거들어요 together.

entries.explanation: 양보하다 (yangbohada) means "to yield / to give way". Start from the polite form 양보해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 양보하다. usagePhrases.en: I do not yield / to give way.
I want to yield / to give way.
I can yield / to give way.
I have to yield / to give way.

usagePhrases.note: Asking someone to offer a seat — often to an elderly or pregnant passenger on the subway.

examples.en: I gave up my seat to an elderly woman on the subway.
examples.note: Classic 양보 scene; 께 is the honorific marker for the older person.

examples.en: It's nice if we each give a little, right?
examples.note: 한 발씩 양보하다 = 'each take a step back / compromise', a set expression.

examples.ko: 운전할 때 양보 운전 좀 해.
examples.romanization: unjeonhal ttae yangbo unjeon jom hae.
examples.en: Drive courteously and yield a bit.
examples.note: 양보 운전 = defensive/courteous driving, letting others merge — useful road vocab.

entries.nuance: 양보하다 covers both physical yielding (a seat, the right of way) and figurative conceding (backing down in an argument, letting someone have their way). entries.shortExplanation: 배웅하다 means "to see someone off" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to see someone off" in Korean is 배웅하다 (baeunghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 배웅해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 배웅하다 for study notes. usagePhrases.note: Politely telling a host not to walk you out; 나오다 = come out (to the door/gate).

examples.en: I was sad my friend was leaving, so I saw them off at the station.
examples.note: 배웅하다 = accompany someone leaving to the door/station; warm farewell gesture.

examples.ko: 할머니가 문 앞까지 나와서 배웅해 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: halmeoniga mun apkkaji nawaseo baeunghae jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Grandma came out to the door to see me off.
examples.note: Common Korean courtesy — older hosts walk guests out; -아/어 주시다 shows the kindness done for you.

examples.ko: 다음에 또 와, 하면서 배웅해 줬어요.
examples.romanization: daeume tto wa, hamyeonseo baeunghae jwosseoyo.
examples.en: They saw me off saying 'come again next time.'
examples.note: Natural parting scene after visiting someone's home.

entries.nuance: 배웅하다 is the counterpart to 마중하다 (meeting an arrival): it means accompanying someone who is leaving — walking them to the door, station, or airport. It signals warmth and respect, and declining a host's 배웅 ('배웅 안 나오셔도 돼요') is itself polite. The noun 배웅 is used freely (배웅 나가다, 배웅 인사).

Use 배웅해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Swapping 배웅하다 (see off / departure) with 마중하다 (meet / arrival) — they're opposites; mixing them up is a classic learner error.

entries.explanation: 맞이하다 (majihada) = "to welcome / to greet (an arrival)". examples.en: To welcome the new year, my family ate rice-cake soup together.
examples.note: N을/를 맞이해서 = 'on the occasion of / to welcome N'; fixed pattern for holidays and events.

examples.en: It feels strange to be about to enter my 30s.
examples.note: 맞이하다 also marks reaching a new stage of life — useful and relatable in your late 20s.

entries.nuance: 맞이하다 means to welcome or receive — both people (greeting an arriving guest) and occasions (a new year, a new phase of life). The everyday spoken cousin is 맞다 ('손님 맞을 준비'), but 맞이하다 is the clearer dictionary verb.

examples.en: I broke my promise again, so my friend got angry.

entries.nuance: 어기다 is the standard verb for breaking something intangible you're bound to keep — a promise (약속), a rule (규칙), a law (법), or a signal (신호). It's the direct antonym of 지키다 (to keep/abide by). Don't use it for physically breaking objects; that's 깨다 or 부수다.

examples.ko: 비밀 꼭 지켜 줄 수 있어?

examples.en: Can you definitely keep this a secret?
examples.note: 비밀을 지키다 = keep a secret; everyday trust vocabulary among friends.

entries.shortExplanation: 베풀다 means "to show kindness / to be generous" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

examples.en: The boss is always generous to the employees.
examples.note: 잘 베풀다 = be generous/giving; describes a warm, open-handed person.

examples.ko: 어려울 때 도움을 베풀어 주셔서 감사해요.
examples.romanization: eoryeoul ttae doumeul bepureo jusyeoseo gamsahaeyo.
examples.en: Thank you for extending help when times were hard.

examples.en: They say what you give to others comes back to you.
examples.note: Common saying about generosity (karma-like); 만큼 = 'as much as'.

entries.nuance: 베풀다 means to give generously of yourself — kindness, help, hospitality, favors — usually from a position of being able to give. Use 베풀어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the formal form as 베풀습니다 — the ㄹ drops, giving 베풉니다.
Using 베풀다 with concrete gifts (선물을 베풀다 sounds odd) — pair it with abstract kindness; use 주다 for objects.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 베풀어 and 베풀어요 together.

entries.explanation: 나누다 (nanuda) means "to share / to divide". Start from the polite form 나눠요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 나누다. usagePhrases.note: Dividing food or a bill evenly with someone; 반씩 = half each.

examples.ko: 피자 한 판 시켜서 친구랑 나눠 먹었어요.
examples.romanization: pija han pan sikyeoseo chingurang nanwo meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: I ordered a pizza and shared it with a friend.
examples.note: 나눠 먹다 = share food; 나누다 + 먹다 is an extremely common everyday combo.

examples.en: We split the bill evenly among the three of us.
examples.note: Splitting the check (n빵/더치페이) — 나누다 is the verb for dividing the cost.

examples.ko: 그 친구랑 고민을 나누면 마음이 편해져요.
examples.romanization: geu chingurang gomineul nanumyeon maeumi pyeonhaejyeoyo.
examples.en: Sharing my worries with that friend puts me at ease.
examples.note: 고민을 나누다 = share one's worries; 나누다 extends to feelings and conversation, not just things.

entries.nuance: 나누다 covers two linked ideas: to divide (split a bill, cut into portions) and to share (food, feelings, conversation). examples.en: I took my grandfather to the hospital.
examples.note: 모시고 가다 = the honorific of 데리고 가다, used when accompanying an elder.

examples.en: I'll show the guest to their seat.
examples.note: Set service phrase in restaurants/hotels; 모시다 elevates the customer respectfully.

examples.en: I drove the boss to the airport.
examples.note: 모셔다 드리다 = escort/drive someone respectfully; standard for superiors at work.

entries.nuance: 모시다 is the honorific verb for accompanying, escorting, taking, or living with someone of higher status — parents, grandparents, bosses, clients, guests. It replaces plain 데리고 가다/오다 (used for peers, children, pets) whenever respect is due. You'll hear it constantly in service settings ('모시겠습니다') and family talk (부모님을 모시다).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 모시다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 모셔요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 데리고 가다 for an elder or boss — that sounds rude; switch to 모시고 가다.
Using 모시다 for friends, children, or pets — it's only for people you must honor; use 데리다 otherwise.

entries.shortExplanation: 권하다 means "to recommend / to offer / to urge" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 권하다 (gwonhada) = "to recommend / to offer / to urge". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 권해요 plus one useful sentence like 이거 한번 권해 드려요 ("I'd recommend trying this"). Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Suggesting a dish or product politely; -아/어 드리다 raises it for the listener.

examples.en: The owner recommended this menu item to me.
examples.note: 권하다 = recommend/suggest; a touch more formal than 추천하다, often face-to-face.

examples.ko: 어른이 술을 권하시면 두 손으로 받아요.
examples.romanization: eoreuni sureul gwonhasimyeon du soneuro badayo.
examples.en: When an elder offers you a drink, receive it with both hands.
examples.note: Key etiquette: 두 손으로 받다 = receive with both hands; essential at any 회식.

examples.en: For your health, I'd like to urge you to quit smoking.
examples.note: 권하다 also = urge/advise a course of action; 금연 = quitting smoking.

entries.nuance: 권하다 spans recommending (a dish, a book), offering (food or a drink to someone), and urging/advising (a course of action). In daily life it's strongly tied to table manners — 술을 권하다 (offering/pressing drinks) is a loaded part of 회식 culture, where refusing politely is its own skill. It's slightly more formal and personal than the neutral 추천하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 권하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 권해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Assuming 권하다 always means a gentle suggestion — 술을 권하다 can mean actively pressing someone to drink, so read the context.

entries.explanation: 사양하다 (sayanghada) means "to politely decline". Start from the polite form 사양해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 사양하다. A strong first sentence is 사양하지 말고 드세요 ("Don't hold back, please eat"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. examples.note: 정중히 사양하다 = decline courteously; useful for refusing drinks at 회식 gracefully.

examples.note: 사양하다 softens a refusal of an invitation/event so it doesn't feel like flat rejection.

entries.nuance: 사양하다 is a courteous, somewhat formal way to decline an offer — food, a drink, a gift, an invitation — without the bluntness of 거절하다 (to reject). The fixed host phrase 사양하지 말고 드세요 ('don't be shy, please eat') is something you'll hear constantly at Korean tables. Because Korean politeness often involves a first refusal, knowing how to 사양하다 gracefully is genuinely useful.

entries.nuance: 근무하다 is the workplace word for 'to work / be on duty', focused on your employment or shift rather than the physical act of doing tasks. entries.nuance: 담당하다 means to officially be responsible for a specific task, client, or area at work. The derived noun 담당자 ('the person in charge') is one of the most-used office words — you'll hear 담당자분께 전달할게요 (I'll pass it to the person in charge) constantly. It implies an assigned, ongoing duty, so it's stronger and more formal than just 하다. Use it to clarify roles, route requests, and introduce who owns what.

entries.nuance: 맡다 is the everyday verb for taking on a role or responsibility — a task, a project, a part of the work. It feels more personal and active than 담당하다 (which is the official 'assigned to'), so volunteering with 제가 맡을게요 sounds proactive and team-friendly. Watch the spelling: the stem ends in ㅌ, giving 맡아요 / 맡았어요 (NOT a ㄷ-irregular). Its causative partner 맡기다 means to entrust the task to someone else.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 맡다 as a complete polite sentence.

Not a ㄷ-irregular: it's 맡아요/맡았어요, never 마라요. Also don't confuse 맡다 (take charge) with 맡기다 (entrust to someone).

entries.nuance: 보고하다 is the formal verb for reporting information up a hierarchy — to a boss, a client, or headquarters. In Korea's hierarchical work culture, 보고 (the report itself) is a big deal, so you'll often use the humble 보고드리다 when reporting to a superior. The recipient takes 께/에게(한테) and the content takes 을/를. For casually telling a peer something, 말하다 or 알려주다 is more natural; save 보고하다 for official updates.

entries.nuance: 진행하다 means to push a task, process, project, or event forward — it's the verb for 'carry out / proceed with' and it's everywhere in Korean office life. entries.nuance: 마치다 means to finish or conclude something properly — your workday, a meeting, a report, a course. It's transitive (you take an object: 일을 마치다) and carries a slightly formal, 'bringing to a proper close' feeling, which is why announcements use 마치겠습니다. The stem ends in ㅊ + ㅣ, so it conjugates 마쳐요 / 마쳤어요. Compare with the more casual, hands-on 끝내다, and the intransitive 끝나다 ('it ends').

Use 마쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
마치다 needs an object (일을 마치다). For 'it ended by itself' use the intransitive 끝나다, not 마치다.

entries.nuance: 끝내다 is the active, everyday verb for finishing or wrapping something up — you make it end. It's the transitive partner of 끝나다 ('it ends on its own'), which is already common: 일을 끝냈어요 (I finished the work) vs. 일이 끝났어요 (the work ended). Compared with 마치다, 끝내다 is more casual and task-focused, perfect for daily office talk like 이것만 끝내고 갈게요. The stem is 끝내- so the past is 끝냈어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 끝내다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 끝내요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't swap 끝내다 (transitive: you finish it) with 끝나다 (intransitive: it finishes): 숙제를 끝냈어요 vs. 수업이 끝났어요.

entries.nuance: 검토하다 means to review or examine something carefully — documents, proposals, plans, contracts — usually before approving or deciding. It's a polished business word, and 검토 중이에요 ('it's under review') is a handy, face-saving way to say a decision hasn't been made yet. It implies careful inspection, not a quick glance, so for casually 'checking' something simple you'd use 확인하다 instead.

entries.nuance: 야근하다 is the verb every office worker in Korea knows: to stay and work past regular hours. entries.nuance: 삐치다 (often spelled/spoken 삐지다) is the everyday word for getting in a sulky huff because your feelings were hurt — someone forgot you, replied late, or left you out. It's lighter and more childish/cute than serious anger, used constantly among friends and couples. 토라지다 emphasizes turning away coldly; 삐치다 just emphasizes the hurt-and-pouty state.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 삐치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 삐쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
삐지다 is the very common spoken variant; both are widely used, but 삐치다 is the standard dictionary form.
Past tense is 삐쳤어요 (삐치 + 었 → 삐쳐 + ㅆ). Don't write it as 삐쳣어요 or 삐쳤써요.

entries.nuance: 골내다 combines being sulky and being irritated — a grumpy, moody upset where someone broods and gives off a sour mood, half-pouting and half-angry. It's stronger and grumpier than 삐치다 but less explosive than 화내다. You'll also hear 골나다 (the intransitive 'to become grumpy') and the noun 골 in 골이 났다.

골내다 (transitive, 'to put out grumpiness') vs 골나다 (to become grumpy) — keep the 내/나 distinction like 화내다/화나다.
Don't confuse 골 (mood/temper here) with 골 meaning 'brain' or 'goal' — context decides.

entries.shortExplanation: 짜증내다 means "to get irritated (and show it)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to get irritated (and show it)" in Korean is 짜증내다 (jjajeungnaeda). entries.nuance: 짜증내다 is to outwardly express irritation/annoyance — snapping, a sharp tone, an exasperated face. It's one of the most-used emotion verbs in daily life, lighter than full anger (화내다) but clearly negative and aimed at someone. Compare 짜증나다 ('to feel/get annoyed', the internal feeling) with 짜증내다 ('to act annoyed at someone').
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 짜증내다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 짜증내요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
짜증내다 (show irritation, transitive-ish) vs 짜증나다 (feel irritated). '나 짜증나' = I'm annoyed; '나한테 짜증내지 마' = don't be snippy at me.
Romanize the double ㅉ as 'jj' — it's a tense consonant, not 'j'.

I can throw a tantrum (demand stubbornly).
I have to throw a tantrum (demand stubbornly).
The kid is throwing a fit demanding I buy a toy.
usagePhrases.note: The textbook scene for 떼쓰다 — a child's nagging demand.

examples.ko: 마트에서 과자 사 달라고 바닥에 누워서 떼썼어요.
examples.romanization: mateueseo gwaja sa dallago badage nuwoseo ttesseosseoyo.
examples.en: He lay on the floor at the mart demanding snacks.
examples.note: 떼썼어요 = past (떼쓰 + 었, ㅡ drops). Very vivid kid behavior.

examples.en: You can't keep throwing tantrums now that you're an adult.

examples.ko: 아무리 떼써도 안 되는 건 안 돼.
examples.romanization: amuri ttesseodo an doeneun geon an dwae.
examples.en: No matter how much you whine for it, no means no.

entries.nuance: 떼쓰다 is to insistently, unreasonably demand something — the whining, foot-stamping, won't-take-no kind of behavior, prototypically by a child but also said of adults acting childishly. It centers on stubborn demanding rather than sadness or quiet sulking. Pairs constantly with -아/어 달라고 (asking for something to be done).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 떼쓰다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 떼써요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
쓰다 here follows the ㅡ-irregular: stem 떼쓰- + 어 → 떼써, past 떼썼어요. Don't write 떼쓰어요.
It's 떼쓰다, not 때쓰다 — the vowel is ㅔ (떼 = a fit/unreasonable demand).
notes: ㅡ: memorize 떼써 and 떼써요 together.

entries.shortExplanation: 비웃다 means "to sneer at (laugh at scornfully)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
