examples.romanization: bareumi isanghadago biuseulkka bwa mareul mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: I couldn't speak up, afraid they'd laugh at my pronunciation.
examples.note: Very real fear for language learners; -을까 봐 = afraid that.

examples.ko: 남을 비웃는 사람은 결국 신뢰를 잃어요.
examples.romanization: nameul biunneun sarameun gyeolguk silloereul ireoyo.
examples.en: People who sneer at others end up losing trust.
examples.note: Moral-tone sentence; 남을 비웃다 = mock others.

examples.en: He scoffed and sneered at my plan.
examples.note: 콧방귀를 뀌다 (to scoff) pairs idiomatically with 비웃다.

entries.nuance: 비웃다 is to laugh at someone scornfully — to mock, sneer, or ridicule, looking down on them. The 비- prefix (from 비방/비하 nuance) turns plain 웃다 (to laugh) into contemptuous laughter. It's distinctly negative and hurtful, unlike 놀리다 which can be playful teasing.

비웃다 is scornful/mean; for light, friendly teasing use 놀리다 instead, or you'll sound harsher than intended.

entries.nuance: 벌다 is the everyday verb for earning or making money through work or income — 돈을 벌다 is the core phrase. entries.nuance: 낭비하다 means to waste or squander a resource — money, time, energy — and always carries a clearly negative, wasteful tone. As a 하다 verb it conjugates regularly: 낭비해요, 낭비했어요, 낭비합니다. Its opposites are 아끼다 (be frugal) and 절약 (saving).

entries.nuance: 갚다 means to pay back what you owe — money (돈, 카드값, 대출, 빚) or, figuratively, a favor or kindness (은혜를 갚다). It is the natural counterpart to 빌리다 (to borrow). commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 갚다 as a complete polite sentence.

entries.nuance: 맡기다 means to entrust or hand something over into someone's care — money to a bank (돈을 은행에 맡기다 = deposit), bags to a counter, dry cleaning to a shop, or a job to a person. For purely financial deposits you may also hear 예금하다, but 맡기다 is the warm, everyday word.

entries.shortExplanation: 흥정하다 means "to haggle" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to haggle" in Korean is 흥정하다 (heungjeonghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 흥정해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 흥정하다 for study notes. entries.nuance: 흥정하다 is to bargain or negotiate over a price, going back and forth until both sides agree — natural at traditional markets, in secondhand deals (중고거래), and for big buys like a used car. It describes the whole negotiation, whereas 깎다 is the concrete act of getting the price knocked down. Note that fixed-price stores (정찰제) like department stores or franchises don't allow it: 흥정 안 돼요. As a 하다 verb it is regular: 흥정해요, 흥정했어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 흥정하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 흥정해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Treating 흥정하다 and 깎다 as identical — 흥정하다 is the negotiating process, 깎다 is actually lowering the price.

entries.nuance: 보태다 means to add money or resources to make up a shortfall or supplement an amount — chipping in for a shared gift, helping with living costs, topping up someone's allowance. beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 남의 휴대폰을 엿보면 안 돼요. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 안 엿봐요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 엿볼 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 엿봐요 feels easy, practice 엿보고 싶어요, 엿볼 수 있어요, and 엿봐야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

classroomScript: Teacher says: 엿봐요. Learner repeats three times.
Teacher asks a yes/no question with 남의 휴대폰을 엿보면 안 돼요. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 안 엿봐요, then 엿볼 수 없어요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

miniDialogue.en: Peeking at the next person's answer sheet is cheating

miniDialogue.en: Shall we peek / spy on?

drills.en: I do not peek / spy on.
drills.note: Change the polite present into a simple negative.

drills.en: I want to peek / spy on.
drills.note: Change the verb into a desire sentence.
Use this for inability or a real limitation.

selfCheck: Can you say “I peek / spy on” politely?
Can you say “I want to peek / spy on”?
Can you explain the difference between 안 엿봐요 and 엿볼 수 없어요?

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 엿보다 becomes 엿볼 수 있어요 ("can") and 엿볼 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

entries.shortExplanation: 노려보다 means "to glare at" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 노려보다 (noryeoboda) means "to glare at". Start from the polite form 노려봐요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 노려보다. A strong first sentence is 왜 그렇게 노려봐요? ("Why are you glaring at me like that?"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 노려보다 also becomes 노려보고 싶어요 (want), 노려볼 수 있어요 (can), and 노려볼 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 노려봐요. Then practice 안 노려봐요 vs 노려볼 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.
survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.en: Why are you glaring at me like that?

examples.en: Everyone glared at the person who cut in line

examples.ko: 강아지가 낯선 사람을 가만히 노려보고 있었어요
examples.romanization: gangajiga natseon sarameul gamanhi noryeobogo isseosseoyo
examples.en: The dog was quietly glaring at the stranger
Maybe they were angry — they glared at me for a while

entries.nuance: 노려보다 is to stare at someone with anger or hostility — to glare. It's strong and clearly negative, signaling irritation, threat, or a challenge. Use it only when you really mean an angry stare; for a plain look use 보다, and for an uncomfortable lingering look use 쳐다보다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 노려보다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 노려봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
노려보다 is never neutral — don't use it where English 'look at' would do.

lesson.canDo: Use 노려봐요 in a real beginner sentence, then change it into want, can, cannot, and have-to forms without losing the basic meaning.
studyFlow: Say 노려봐요 first. This is the safest spoken form for most beginner situations.
Add one useful frame: 왜 그렇게 노려봐요?. Read the Hangul first, then check the romanization.
Practice the contrast between 안 노려봐요 and 노려볼 수 없어요.

lesson.teacherNote: Do not ask a beginner to memorize all 15 forms at once. Teach 노려봐요 first, then add one communicative need: desire (노려보고 싶어요), possibility (노려볼 수 있어요), or limitation (노려볼 수 없어요).
lesson.pronunciationTip: 노려보다 is written noryeoboda. In real sentences, compare the audio with the romanization because Korean sound changes can cross syllable blocks.

entries.shortExplanation: 훑어보다 means "to skim / look over quickly" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to skim / look over quickly" in Korean is 훑어보다 (hulteoboda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 훑어봐요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 훑어보다 for study notes. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

examples.en: I skim the news on my way to work
Don't just skim the contract — read it carefully
The interviewer skimmed down my resume
examples.note: 쭉 훑어보다 = run one's eyes over

entries.nuance: 훑어보다 means to run your eyes over something quickly to get the gist — skimming a menu, an article, or a document. It implies speed and a lack of deep attention, so it pairs naturally with 쓱 or 쭉, and contrasts with 살펴보다 (careful inspection).

Use 훑어봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 훑어보다 when you mean to read or check something thoroughly — use 살펴보다 or 읽다.

entries.shortExplanation: 엿듣다 means "to eavesdrop / overhear" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 엿듣다 (yeotdeutda) = "to eavesdrop / overhear". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 엿들어요 plus one useful sentence like 남의 대화를 엿듣지 마세요 ("Don't eavesdrop on other people's conversations"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 엿듣고 싶어요 for what you want, 엿들을 수 있어요 for what you can, 엿들을 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: 엿듣다 = listen in secretly (ㄷ irregular: 듣다→들어요)

examples.ko: 카페에서 옆자리 얘기를 본의 아니게 엿들었어요
examples.romanization: kapeeseo yeopjari yaegireul bonui anige yeotdeureosseoyo
examples.en: At the cafe I unintentionally overheard the next table's talk
I got caught eavesdropping at the door

examples.ko: 남의 통화를 엿듣는 건 예의가 아니에요
examples.romanization: namui tonghwareul yeotdeunneun geon yeuiga anieyo
examples.en: Listening in on someone's call isn't polite

entries.nuance: 엿듣다 is the listening counterpart of 엿보다 — to overhear or eavesdrop, usually secretly. Like its English equivalent it sounds improper, so people often soften it with 우연히 ('by chance') or 본의 아니게 ('unintentionally') to make clear it wasn't deliberate. It follows the ㄷ-irregular: 듣다 → 들어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 엿듣다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 엿들어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Remember the ㄷ irregular: it's 엿들어요 / 엿들었어요, never 엿듣어요.
notes: ㄷ: memorize 엿들어 and 엿들어요 together.

I want to understand (by hearing) / catch what is said.
I can understand (by hearing) / catch what is said.
I have to understand (by hearing) / catch what is said.
I couldn't catch what you were saying
usagePhrases.note: The single most useful phrase for learners (ㄷ irregular)

examples.ko: 한국어를 다 알아듣지는 못하지만 조금은 알아들어요
examples.romanization: hangugeoreul da aradeutjineun motajiman jogeumeun aradeureoyo
examples.en: I can't catch all the Korean, but I understand a little
The pronunciation was so fast I couldn't catch a thing
examples.note: 하나도 못 알아듣다 = not catch a single word

examples.en: Even the dog understands its own name

entries.nuance: 알아듣다 is to understand something you hear — to catch or make out spoken words. It's distinct from 이해하다 (to comprehend a concept): 알아듣다 is specifically about successfully receiving speech. For anyone living in Korea, '못 알아들었어요' and '천천히 말해 주세요' are everyday survival lines. It follows the ㄷ-irregular: 듣다 → 들어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 알아듣다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 알아들어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
ㄷ irregular: say 알아들어요 / 알아들었어요, not 알아듣어요. Also don't replace it with 이해하다 when you mean catching spoken words.
notes: ㄷ: memorize 알아들어 and 알아들어요 together.

usagePhrases.note: 놓치다 = fail to catch a bus, train, or chance.

entries.nuance: 놓치다 is for missing something you were trying to catch — a bus, a train, or a chance — and it always takes 을/를. Don't confuse it with 보고 싶다 (to miss a person). It's a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 놓치 + 어 → 놓쳐요. It often appears with 늦다 (to be late) in everyday excuses.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 놓치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 놓쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
To say you miss a PERSON, use 보고 싶다, not 놓치다 — 놓치다 is only for missing a bus, chance, etc.

entries.nuance: 세우다 is the transitive 'stand something up / bring it to a stop' — most usefully, telling a taxi driver to stop: 여기 세워 주세요. It's the causative pair of 서다 (to stand/stop, by itself). Because the stem ends in 우, 우 + 어 contracts to 워, giving 세워요 and past 세웠어요. Beginners should memorize 세워 주세요 as a ready-made phrase for taxis.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 세우다 as a complete polite sentence.

entries.shortExplanation: 다가가다 means "to go closer / to approach" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 다가가다 (dagagada) means "to go closer / to approach". Start from the polite form 다가가요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 다가가다. Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I do not go closer / to approach.
I want to go closer / to approach.
I can go closer / to approach.
I have to go closer / to approach.

usagePhrases.note: 다가가다 = move closer toward something/someone else.

examples.en: I slowly approached the cat.
I go closer to the window.
Approach carefully.

entries.nuance: 다가가다 is the 'going' counterpart of 다가오다: you move closer toward a target that is away from the speaker. Think 가다 (go) plus 'closer'. For something approaching toward you, switch to 다가오다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 다가가다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 다가가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 다가가다 when something moves toward you — that is 다가오다.

beginnerPath.body: 다가가요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 다가가다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 천천히 다가가요. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 안 다가가요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 다가갈 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns

entries.nuance: 세탁하다 means to launder or wash clothes, from the Sino-Korean noun 세탁 plus 하다. entries.nuance: 정돈하다 means to put things in neat order — straightening, lining up, and arranging items into place. It overlaps with 정리하다, but 정돈하다 leans toward making things look tidy and orderly, while 정리하다 leans toward sorting out and clearing away. You'll often see them together as the set phrase 정리정돈 ('tidying and ordering').
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 정돈하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 정돈해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
정돈하다 is about arranging neatly, not throwing things away — to clear/sort out, 정리하다 fits better.

entries.nuance: 꾸미다 covers both decorating a space (방을 꾸미다) and dressing yourself up to look nice (예쁘게 꾸미다). It is a regular ㅣ-stem verb, so 꾸미 + 어 contracts to 꾸며 → 꾸며요, past 꾸몄어요. The thing you decorate takes 을/를, and you often add an adverb like 예쁘게 ('prettily') or 멋있게 ('stylishly').

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.
survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.note: 소원을 빌다 = to make a wish, a very common collocation.

examples.en: I made a wish at New Year
I pray for my family's health

examples.ko: 시험 잘 보라고 행운을 빌어 줄게요
examples.romanization: siheom jal borago haenguneul bireo julgeyo
examples.en: I'll wish you luck on your test
examples.note: 빌어 주다 = to wish on someone's behalf.

entries.nuance: 빌다 means to pray, wish, or plead for something, as in 소원을 빌다 (make a wish) and 행운을 빌다 (wish luck). It is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the stem ㄹ drops before ㄴ, ㅂ, and ㅅ endings, so the formal form is 빕니다 and the future is 빌 거예요 (no doubled ㄹ). Note that 빌다 can also mean 'to borrow' in older usage, but modern Korean uses 빌리다 for borrowing.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 빌다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 빌어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the formal form as 빌습니다 — the ㄹ drops, so it is 빕니다.
Confusing 빌다 (to pray / wish) with 빌리다 (to borrow).
notes: ㄹ: memorize 빌어 and 빌어요 together.

lesson.canDo: Use 빌어요 in a real beginner sentence, then change it into want, can, cannot, and have-to forms without losing the basic meaning.
studyFlow: Say 빌어요 first. This is the safest spoken form for most beginner situations.
Add one useful frame: 소원을 빌어요. Read the Hangul first, then check the romanization.
Practice the contrast between 빌지 않아요 and 빌 수 없어요.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 빌어요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 빌다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 소원을 빌어요. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 빌지 않아요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 빌 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 빌어요 feels easy, practice 빌고 싶어요, 빌 수 있어요, and 빌어야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

Learner changes the sentence to 빌지 않아요, then 빌 수 없어요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 빌다 becomes 빌 수 있어요 ("can") and 빌 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

entries.shortExplanation: 기르다 means "to grow" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 기르다 (gireuda) means "to grow". Start from the polite form 길러요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 기르다. Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 기르다 means to grow, raise, or cultivate — hair, plants, animals, and even habits or abilities. It is a 르-irregular verb: before an 아/어 ending the 르 becomes ㄹㄹ, so 기르 + 어 turns into 길러, and the past is 길렀어요. It overlaps with 키우다, but 기르다 is preferred for hair and beard.

Use 길러요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the past as 기르었어요 — the 르 irregular makes it 길렀어요.
Forgetting the doubled ㄹ: the casual form is 길러, not 기러.

entries.shortExplanation: 낳다 means "to give birth" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to give birth" in Korean is 낳다 (nata). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 낳아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 낳다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 아기를 낳아요 ("I give birth to a baby") — then reshape the same stem into 낳고 싶어요 (desire), 낳을 수 있어요 (ability), and 낳을 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

Dropping the ㅎ and writing 나아요; the correct polite form is 낳아요.

entries.nuance: 닮다 means to resemble or take after someone, in looks or character. Korean usually states resemblance in the past tense — 닮았어요 ('looks like') describes a present fact, much like English 'looks like'. The object of resemblance takes 을/를, or you can pair people with 하고/와/과.

Saying 닮아요 for 'looks like' — Koreans normally use the past 닮았어요 for a present resemblance.
Using 같다 (to be the same) when you mean only a resemblance, which is 닮다.

I want to occur, to happen, to arise.

usagePhrases.note: 발생하다 = (a problem/event) comes into being. The thing that occurs takes 이/가, never 을/를. More formal than 생기다.

examples.en: An error occurred during payment.
examples.note: 발생했습니다 (formal) is the standard wording you see on screens and official notices.

examples.note: 비용이 발생하다 = a cost arises — set phrase for fees and surcharges.

examples.note: Conditional 발생하면 is everyday phrasing; a notch more formal than 생기면.

entries.nuance: 발생하다 is a formal, written-leaning verb for an event, problem, or phenomenon coming into existence — accidents, errors, fires, costs, diseases. Writing 발생하요 instead of 발생해요 — 하다 always contracts to 해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 존재하다 means "to exist" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 존재하다 (jonjaehada) means "to exist". Start from the polite form 존재해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 존재하다. examples.note: Formal 존재합니다 fits essays and serious discussion about society.

entries.nuance: 존재하다 means 'to exist' in an abstract or emphatic sense, common in writing, debate, and serious topics. For everyday 'there is / I have,' Koreans use 있다 (책이 있어요), not 존재하다. Reach for 존재하다 when you want to stress the very existence of something — a method, a being, a problem — or to deny it flatly with 존재하지 않아요. It is intransitive; the thing that exists takes 이/가.

Don't replace everyday 있다 with 존재하다 — 'I have a question' is 질문이 있어요, not 질문이 존재해요.
The natural negative is 존재하지 않아요; '존재 안 해요' sounds clipped and off-register for this abstract verb.

examples.en: The two countries maintain a friendly relationship.

entries.nuance: 유지하다 means to keep something the way it is so it doesn't change or decline — health, temperature, grades, balance, relationships. examples.ko: 이 앱으로 대부분의 문제를 해결할 수 있어요.

examples.en: We resolved the conflict through dialogue.

entries.nuance: 해결하다 is the everyday and formal verb for solving or settling a problem, conflict, or issue — by far its most common partner is 문제 (문제를 해결하다). It's transitive (을/를). commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 해결하다 as a complete polite sentence.

It's transitive — say 문제를 해결했어요, not 문제가 해결했어요 (for 'the problem was solved,' use 해결됐어요).
For math problems or riddles specifically, 풀다 is also natural (문제를 풀다); 해결하다 suits real-life issues and disputes.

examples.en: Housing costs make up a large part of spending.
examples.note: 큰 부분을 차지하다 = account for a large share — common in budget talk.

examples.en: That singer took the number one spot.
examples.note: For rankings and charts — 1위를/정상을 차지하다 (take first place / the top).

examples.en: The luggage takes up too much space.
examples.note: 자리를 차지하다 = take up space/a seat — literal, everyday use too.

entries.nuance: 차지하다 has two everyday senses: to take up a proportion or amount (식비가 절반을 차지하다 = food is half the cost) and to secure or win something (1위를 차지하다 = take first place). It's transitive — the share or prize taken takes 을/를. The first sense is great for talking about budgets and statistics ('X accounts for Y%'); the second is common in sports, charts, and competitions.

It's transitive — mark the share/rank with 을/를: 절반을 차지하다, 1위를 차지하다.
Don't confuse the 'win a rank' sense with 이기다 (to beat an opponent); 차지하다 is about securing the position/share itself.

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

entries.shortExplanation: 경쟁하다 means "to compete" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to compete" in Korean is 경쟁하다 (gyeongjaenghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 경쟁해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 경쟁하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 치열하게 경쟁해요 ("They compete fiercely") — then reshape the same stem into 경쟁하고 싶어요 (desire), 경쟁할 수 있어요 (ability), and 경쟁 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 경쟁해요. Then practice 경쟁 안 해요 vs 경쟁 못 해요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.
survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.note: 치열하다 (fierce/intense) is the go-to adverb with 경쟁하다 to describe tough rivalry.

examples.ko: 요즘 회사들이 가격으로 심하게 경쟁하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum hoesadeuri gagyeogeuro simhage gyeongjaenghago isseoyo.
examples.en: These days companies are competing hard on price.
examples.note: (으)로 marks what they compete on; 경쟁하고 있다 (ongoing) shows it's a current situation.

examples.ko: 같은 자리를 두고 여러 명이 경쟁했어요.
examples.romanization: gateun jarireul dugo yeoreo myeongi gyeongjaenghaesseoyo.
examples.en: Several people competed for the same position.
examples.note: N을/를 두고 경쟁하다 = 'to compete over N', a natural pattern for a prize, spot, or position.

examples.en: It's better to cooperate than to compete with each other.
examples.note: Pairs naturally with 협력하다 as its opposite; -기보다 contrasts the two choices.

entries.nuance: 경쟁하다 describes rivalry where parties try to outdo each other for the same goal, prize, or market, and it carries a neutral-to-tense feeling depending on context. The rival is marked with 와/과, and what you compete over uses 을/를 두고. The noun 경쟁 is everywhere in daily life: 경쟁률 (competition ratio), 입시 경쟁 (exam competition), 경쟁사 (a competitor company).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 경쟁하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 경쟁해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 경쟁을 이겨요 to mean 'win the competition' — use 경쟁에서 이기다 (win in the competition); 경쟁 itself is the act of competing, not the contest you defeat.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 치열하게 경쟁해요. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 경쟁 안 해요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 경쟁 못 해요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 경쟁해요 feels easy, practice 경쟁하고 싶어요, 경쟁할 수 있어요, and 경쟁해야 돼요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

Teacher asks a yes/no question with 치열하게 경쟁해요. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 경쟁 안 해요, then 경쟁 못 해요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

entries.english: to participate / to take part in
entries.shortExplanation: 참여하다 means "to participate / to take part in" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 참여하다 (chamyeohada) = "to participate / to take part in". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 참여해요 plus one useful sentence like 행사에 참여해요 ("I take part in the event"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 참여하고 싶어요 for what you want, 참여할 수 있어요 for what you can, 참여 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

I do not participate / to take part in.
I want to participate / to take part in.
I can participate / to take part in.
I have to participate / to take part in.
I take part in the event
usagePhrases.note: 참여하다 takes 에 for what you join: 토론에 참여해요 = I take part in the discussion.

examples.en: I actively took part in this volunteer activity.
examples.note: 적극적으로 (actively) is a common collocation; 참여하다 stresses involvement, not mere attendance.

examples.ko: 온라인 설문에 누구나 참여할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: ollain seolmune nuguna chamyeohal su isseoyo.
examples.en: Anyone can participate in the online survey.
examples.note: 참여하다 covers joining in an activity, vote, or survey — contributing, not just being present.

examples.ko: 회의에 참여는 했지만 의견은 안 냈어요.
examples.romanization: hoeuie chamyeoneun haetjiman uigyeoneun an naesseoyo.
examples.en: I took part in the meeting but didn't give an opinion.
examples.note: 참여 + 했다 split by 는 adds contrast; shows 참여하다 means active involvement you can still hold back from.

entries.nuance: 참여하다 means actively taking part and contributing to an activity, event, or process, so it emphasizes involvement rather than physically being in a place. Compare it with 참석하다 (to attend), which is just showing up to a meeting or ceremony: you can 참석 a wedding but you 참여 a project. What you join is marked with 에, and the noun 참여 appears in 참여율 (participation rate) and 시민 참여 (citizen participation).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 참여하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 참여해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Mixing up 참여하다 and 참석하다 — use 참석하다 for simply attending a meeting/ceremony, and 참여하다 when you actually get involved and contribute.

entries.shortExplanation: 책임지다 means "to take responsibility" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 책임지다 (chaegimjida) means "to take responsibility". Start from the polite form 책임져요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 책임지다. A strong first sentence is 제가 책임질게요 ("I'll take responsibility"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 책임지다 also becomes 책임지고 싶어요 (want), 책임질 수 있어요 (can), and 책임 못 져요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 책임져요. Then practice 책임 안 져요 vs 책임 못 져요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.
survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.note: Strong, accountable statement; said when you promise to own the outcome of something.

examples.ko: 이 일은 제가 맡았으니까 끝까지 책임지겠습니다.
examples.romanization: i ireun jega matasseunikka kkeutkkaji chaegimjigetseumnida.
examples.en: I took on this task, so I'll take full responsibility for it.
examples.note: 책임지겠습니다 (formal will) is a firm workplace promise to own the result.

examples.en: Who's going to take responsibility for this accident?
examples.note: 책임지다 takes the matter as a direct object (을/를): 사고를 책임지다 = be answerable for the accident.

examples.ko: 부모는 자식을 끝까지 책임져야 한다고 생각해요.
examples.romanization: bumoneun jasigeul kkeutkkaji chaegimjyeoya handago saenggakaeyo.
examples.en: I think parents should be responsible for their children to the end.
examples.note: Also covers taking care of / providing for someone, not only owning up to a mistake.

entries.nuance: 책임지다 (literally 책임 'responsibility' + 지다 'to carry') means to take on and own the consequences of something — a mistake, a task, or even caring for a person. It is heavier and more accountable than just 맡다 (to take charge of): 책임지다 implies you'll answer for how it turns out. Because 지다 is the verb stem, conjugate it as 책임져요 / 책임졌어요, and you can split the noun off (책임 안 져요) in negatives.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 책임지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 책임져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 책임집니다 but then forming the casual as '책임지어요' — the 지다 stem contracts to 져, so it's 책임져요, not 책임지어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 의지하다 means "to rely on / to lean on (emotionally)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

I want to rely on / to lean on (emotionally).
I can rely on / to lean on (emotionally).
I have to rely on / to lean on (emotionally).

usagePhrases.note: Common advice about not relying on someone emotionally or financially to an unhealthy degree.

examples.en: When I was struggling, I relied on my friend a lot.
examples.note: 한테/에게 marks who you lean on; 의지하다 carries a warm, emotional dependence.

examples.ko: 남에게만 의지하지 말고 스스로 해 보세요.
examples.romanization: namegeman uijihaji malgo seuseuro hae boseyo.
examples.en: Don't just depend on others — try doing it yourself.
examples.note: Contrasts 의지하다 with being independent (스스로); gentle nudge toward self-reliance.

examples.en: Grandmother walks leaning on a cane.
examples.note: 의지하다 also works physically (leaning on an object for support), here with 에 for the cane.

entries.nuance: 의지하다 means to depend on or lean on someone or something for emotional, practical, or even physical support, and it usually carries a warm, human feeling of trust. Use 에게/한테 for a person and 에 for an object you physically lean on. Note that 'let's rely' (shallWe) is unnatural since reliance isn't something you propose doing together, so that form is left out; emotionally it overlaps with 기대다 (to lean on), which can sound even more intimate.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 의지하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 의지해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the person you rely on with 을/를 (의지를 해요) — the dependable person takes 에게/한테, as in 부모님께 의지해요, not 부모님을 의지해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 존경하다 means "to respect / to look up to" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.en: I respect / to look up to.
I do not respect / to look up to.
I want to respect / to look up to.
I can respect / to look up to.
I have to respect / to look up to.

usagePhrases.note: Sincere expression of deep admiration; stronger than just liking or approving of someone.

examples.en: I respect that person who always takes on challenges.
examples.note: 존경하다 takes the admired person as a direct object (을/를) and conveys looking up to their character.

examples.en: I listened to the teacher's words with a feeling of respect.
examples.note: 존경하는 마음 (a respectful heart) is a natural noun phrase showing the attitude behind the action.

examples.ko: 그렇게 행동하시는 걸 보니 더 존경하게 됐어요.
examples.romanization: geureoke haengdonghasineun geol boni deo jongyeonghage dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: Seeing them act that way, I came to respect them even more.
examples.note: 존경하게 되다 = 'to come to respect', marking a change in feeling triggered by what you saw.

entries.nuance: 존경하다 is deep respect and admiration for a person's character, achievements, or values — looking up to someone, often an elder, mentor, or role model. The admired person takes 을/를, and the modifier form 존경하는 (respected) is a common, slightly formal way to refer to that person.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 존경하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 존경해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 존경하다 (look up to a person) with 존중하다 (respect a decision/opinion) — you 존중 someone's 의견, but you 존경 a person you admire.

entries.english: to ignore / to look down on
entries.shortExplanation: 무시하다 means "to ignore / to look down on" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 무시하다 (musihada) means "to ignore / to look down on". Start from the polite form 무시해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 무시하다. usagePhrases.en: I ignore / to look down on.
I do not ignore / to look down on.
I want to ignore / to look down on.
I can ignore / to look down on.
I have to ignore / to look down on.

usagePhrases.note: Common advice to brush off rude comments or trolls; 그냥 무시해 = don't even react.

examples.en: I just ignored what that person said.
examples.note: 무시하다 + 을/를 = to disregard; here it's choosing not to pay attention to a comment.

examples.en: It's dangerous to ignore the signal and cross the road.
examples.note: Also used for ignoring rules, warnings, or signals — disregarding something you should heed.

examples.ko: 돈이 없다고 사람을 무시하면 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: doni eopsdago sarameul musihamyeon an dwaeyo.
examples.en: You shouldn't look down on people just because they have no money.
examples.note: This sense (belittle/disrespect) is hurtful; 무시당하다 (to be looked down on) is the common passive.

entries.nuance: 무시하다 has two linked senses: (1) to ignore or disregard something — a comment, rule, or warning — and (2) to look down on or belittle a person, which is quite offensive. Context decides which: 신호를 무시하다 is just disregarding a signal, but 사람을 무시하다 means treating someone as inferior. The passive 무시당하다 (to be ignored / be looked down on) is very common when describing being slighted.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 무시하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 무시해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Assuming 무시하다 only means 'ignore' — toward a person it often means 'look down on/disrespect', so 나를 무시하지 마 is a strong 'don't belittle me', not just 'don't ignore me'.

entries.english: to discuss / to talk over (to decide)
entries.shortExplanation: 의논하다 means "to discuss / to talk over (to decide)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to discuss / to talk over (to decide)" in Korean is 의논하다 (uinonhada). The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

I do not discuss / to talk over (to decide).
I want to discuss / to talk over (to decide).
I can discuss / to talk over (to decide).
I have to discuss / to talk over (to decide).

usagePhrases.note: 의논하다 takes 와/과 for the other person and 에 대해 for the topic you discuss to decide.

examples.ko: 이 문제는 부모님과 의논해 보고 결정할게요.
examples.romanization: i munjeneun bumonimgwa uinonhae bogo gyeoljeonghalgeyo.
examples.en: I'll talk this over with my parents and then decide.
examples.note: 와/과 marks who you consult; 의논하다 implies discussing in order to reach a decision.

examples.en: I discussed my career path with my teacher.
examples.note: N에 대해 의논하다 = to talk over the matter of N; common for seeking advice on a choice.

examples.en: Let's not decide alone — let's discuss it together.
examples.note: 의논합시다 (formal 'let's') is natural when proposing a joint discussion before deciding.

entries.nuance: 의논하다 is to talk something over with someone in order to reach a decision or get advice, so it implies a practical, two-way consultation rather than a formal debate. It overlaps with 상의하다 (to consult), which sounds a touch more formal, and contrasts with 토론하다 (to debate a topic from sides). The person you consult takes 와/과 and the topic takes 에 대해; you 'discuss with' family, a partner, or a mentor before settling something.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 의논하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 의논해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the discussion partner with 에게/한테 — 의논하다 uses 와/과 (친구와 의논해요), since you talk things over together, not deliver something one-way.

usagePhrases.en: I trust (firmly) / to have confidence in.
I do not trust (firmly) / to have confidence in.
I want to trust (firmly) / to have confidence in.
I can trust (firmly) / to have confidence in.
I have to trust (firmly) / to have confidence in.

usagePhrases.note: 신뢰하다 takes the trusted person/thing as 을/를; firmer and more formal than 믿다.

examples.ko: 저는 그 회사를 오래전부터 신뢰해 왔어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun geu hoesareul oraejeonbuteo silloehae wasseoyo.
examples.en: I've trusted that company for a long time.
examples.note: 신뢰해 오다 (have been trusting) shows a trust built up over time, typical for brands or institutions.

examples.ko: 한 번 거짓말을 하면 더 이상 신뢰하기 어려워요.
examples.romanization: han beon geojinmareul hamyeon deo isang silloehagi eoryeowoyo.
examples.en: Once someone lies, it's hard to trust them anymore.
examples.note: 신뢰하다 here is firm, reasoned confidence that breaks when betrayed; heavier than casual 믿다.

examples.ko: 팀원들이 서로 신뢰해야 일이 잘 돼요.
examples.romanization: timwondeuri seoro silloehaeya iri jal dwaeyo.
examples.en: Team members have to trust each other for work to go well.
examples.note: Common in work contexts about reliability; the noun 신뢰 means 'trust/confidence'.

entries.nuance: 신뢰하다 is firm, reasoned trust or confidence in a person, organization, or system, and it sounds more formal and weighty than the everyday verb 믿다 (to believe/trust). You 신뢰 a colleague's competence, a company, or a system; you 믿다 a friend, a rumor, or a religion. The trusted target takes 을/를, and the noun 신뢰 (신뢰 관계 = a relationship of trust, 신뢰를 쌓다 = to build trust) is extremely common in work and social writing.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 참석하다 becomes 참석할 수 있어요 ("can") and 참석할 거예요 ("will").
